#5296. Rivian spinout Also was working on an e-moto project in Kenya — until it walked away

Also, the micromobility startup spun out of Rivian in 2025, quietly started and then walked away from an electric two-wheeler pilot project in Kenya earlier this year, as it sought to focus its resources on its consumer e-bike and autonomous vehicle ambitions, TechCrunch has learned.

The project received grant funding from the Shell Foundation, an independent charity established by the British oil and gas giant Shell plc. A section of the Shell Foundation’s website that has since been removed said the project’s goal was to “enable and de-risk global OEM entry into Africa’s EV market by piloting a locally integrated electric two-wheeler platform in Kenya, with potential to scale across East Africa.”

According to the deleted section, Also was expected to work on modular battery designs and distributed EV charging, and planned on “developing a purpose-built electric motorcycle for African riders.”

The opportunity for electric motorcycles seems ripe on the continent, which has a massive two-wheeler market. African mobility company Spiro recently said it has more than 130,000 electric motorcycles operating across seven countries, along with 2,500 battery-swapping stations. This boom has drawn interest from Chinese mobility companies and investors, which are pouring resources into the space.

In a September email, Also told TechCrunch that it had “explored this project” with an unnamed partner, but ultimately “decided to focus on its core roadmap” after completing only “some early-stage work.” Also said the grant funding it received from the Shell Foundation “will follow the project to support its ongoing development,” but declined to offer specifics.

The Shell Foundation told TechCrunch in an email that the project was “intended to generate evidence on driver income uplift potential, operational performance and commercial viability to deepen the company’s understanding of the market opportunity.” But when TechCrunch asked for more specifics, the Shell Foundation declined, citing a nondisclosure agreement with Also. Days later, the project disappeared from the Shell Foundation’s website.

During an interview last month at TechCrunch Disrupt, Also co-founder and president Chris Yu said the Kenya pilot project initially made sense given Also’s mission to build small, purpose-built vehicles that are “first and foremost cost-optimized to do the job that needs to be done in a particular market.”

But other projects took precedence, Yu said, especially the development of small autonomous vehicles — which Also is working on as part of a partnership with DoorDash.

“We piloted and ultimately decided, largely because of just urgency and pace around autonomy, frankly, that our attention would be best, in the near term, served fully focused” on that, he said, adding that he thinks there’s a “high chance that autonomy will show up first, and at a broader scale in these types of purpose-built smaller vehicles than at scale in passenger vehicles.”

Also walked away from the Africa project during a somewhat rocky first year of independence.

Supply chain problems forced the company to repeatedly delay deliveries of its first product, a premium e-bike called the TM-B, frustrating customers who had reserved one. What made matters worse was Also’s relative silence. The company said little for much of 2026 about when the bikes would arrive — a communication failure its leadership now acknowledges was a mistake.

“I think we did a pretty poor job communicating to our reservation holders through the summer when they were all waiting, and we got called out for that,” Yu said in the interview. “But I think it’s actually great. It’s really hard to earn the opportunity for people to care, and to tell us what they think, and to help us improve.”

Getting its first product launch back on track is crucial for Also, which has ambitions far beyond e-bikes. The company plans to sell commercial cargo bikes to companies like Amazon, including four-wheeled models, and has the partnership with DoorDash. These products are next in the company’s pipeline, Yu said, and represent bigger revenue opportunities.

But the TM-B comes first. It’s Also’s most visible product to consumers, and its striking design has drawn plenty of curiosity.

Yu said no single problem was responsible for delaying the bikes, which finally started shipping to customers in early October. Instead, Also spent much of the year playing supply chain Whac-A-Mole, a particularly difficult challenge given the TM-B’s complexity. Yu described the bike as “kind of a computer on wheels.”

At one point, Also found itself competing for the same raw materials used to make printed circuit boards for AI data centers. At other times, the company struggled to navigate certification requirements with different government agencies.

Yu said the scope of these problems, and the pace at which new ones popped up — almost weekly — made it difficult to give customers reliable updates about why their bikes were delayed.

“The entire team is like running at a million miles an hour to get these things produced and shipped to customers, and then it’s also really dynamic as well,” he said. “I think what we could have done better is just [say], straight up: ‘We’re chasing down these things, we’ll have an update shortly.’”

That didn’t happen at first, but Also has steadily improved its communication, earning some goodwill from customers on Reddit. The company will need it as it works through the inevitable kinks that come with a first product. Early customers have already reported problems, including delivery damage and noticeable battery drain.

#5295. AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to $16B as demand surges

Fal, a San Francisco-based startup that hosts and runs AI video, image, and audio models, has raised $1.3 billion in its latest funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Nvidia, Sound Ventures, and T. Rowe Price. The deal values Fal at $16 billion, double its $8 billion valuation in April, Bloomberg reported.

The startup announced its Series E and F rounds at the same time, noting that a combined $1.65 billion was raised across both. (Sequoia led the earlier round.)

The latest round (Series F) comes amid soaring demand for inference services, the process of running an AI model that’s already been trained to generate outputs, particularly from customers relying on open source models. Fal surpassed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year, Bloomberg’s report noted.

Companies providing inference services, including Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Modal, have also been growing rapidly and raising large funding rounds at higher valuations. But their gross margins remain thin because of the high cost of buying or leasing compute, according to several people familiar with inference companies’ financials.

Fal was co-founded in 2021 by Burkay Gur, a former Coinbase machine learning leader and Oracle engineer, and Gorkem Yurtseven, who was previously a developer at Amazon.

Ripple's director of engineering Viijay Khanna directly confirmed that the company is readying 'big plans' for XRP Ledger in 2027. The remark came amid the debates around the blockchain's speed, when critics put the XRP network's stats (around 1,500 transactions per second) against the average daily load of Visa, labeling the XRPL "an outdated copy of legacy payment systems".

"We have big plans for performance improvements lined up for 2027", said Khanna, effectively ending speculations.

The logic is that the basic Layer-1 does not need to digest millions of small transactions directly. Retail microtraffic then goes to the second layer like Dassie (Interledger). The task of the main layer thus becomes maintaining large funds of banks and institutions.

The first step to this kind of independence from "heavy blockchain metal" was made this month with the fresh release of xrpld 3.3.0 which cut the appetite of nodes to RAM by 13-23%.

Technical audits show that the issue was not in simple code flaws, but the caprices of the system's allocator: the software was literally withholding the server's resources after the cache emptying. Bug fix therefore allowed validators to radically decrease infrastructure costs.

For further improvement of the current operational environment on November 4, the network got a fixCleanup package.

Khanna's short commentary is not an attempt to snuff out critics, but a marker of an ecosystem's overhaul for the needs of commercial banks. Ripple's president Monica Long has already announced a plan to relay the big chunk of the company's clients' payments directly on XRP Ledger. Cross-border remittances will be tied to new lending infrastructure as well.

To make sure the network will not flood from institutional funds, XRP Ledger Foundation already presented a 2027 roadmap with these as main highlights:

The overhaul of XRP Ledger is a preventive hit on the network's future overload. Ripple ecosystem builders rewrite the basis, using AI teams for strict testing and code optimization. XRP Ledger is being readied for the moment when transactions with RLUSD stablecoin, tokenized stocks trading, and interbank lending become a routine and not just pilot projects.

#5292. ACryptoS Loses $665K Across 77 Vaults on Five Chains After a Missing Input Check

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit. Five exploiter addresses have been published.A vault is supposed to hand out shares in proportion to what you put in. ACryptoS's vaults handed out most of the pool for the price of one small token deposit, because a function never checked how many amounts it had been given.

ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains. In its announcement on X, the project blamed a lack of input validation that let an attacker mint the majority of a vault's shares by depositing only a minimal amount of tokens.

It then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, said it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database. It traces the bug to the `depositMulti` function, where the length of the amounts array was never verified against the number of tokens. An attacker could deposit a tiny amount of a single token, receive the vast majority of vault shares and then withdraw a proportional share of both tokens. SlowMist lists the affected chains as Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.

Multi-token vaults, like those behind liquidity-pair strategies, take deposits in more than one asset. A function such as `depositMulti` receives a list of amounts, one for each token the vault holds. The contract then values that bundle against the pool and issues shares accordingly.The safeguard is basic: the number of amounts supplied must equal the number of tokens in the vault. When the two don't match, the contract is working from incomplete or mismatched input, and its valuation logic can behave in ways its authors never intended. According to SlowMist, that check was absent.How ordinary this flaw is deserves a mention. It isn't an oracle trick or a flash-loan puzzle. It's a missing `require` statement on a public function, exactly the kind of slip that audits and fuzzing exist to catch.

A simplified illustration shows how the numbers work. ACryptoS's published analysis doesn't include the exact contract code, so what follows describes the mechanics of this class of bug, not a line-by-line reconstruction.In a healthy vault, shares are minted in proportion to the deposit's share of the pool. Suppose a vault holds $10,000 in assets and has issued 10,000 shares. A $1 deposit should mint about 1 share, or 0.01% of the supply, and redeeming those shares returns about $1.Now let mismatched inputs throw off the mint calculation. The ratio of deposit to pool collapses or inverts, and the contract might credit the attacker with 90,000 new shares for that $1. The attacker then holds 90,000 of 100,000 shares, or 90% of the supply. Because withdrawals pay out pro rata, redeeming those shares returns about 90% of each token in the pool, roughly $9,000, for a $1 deposit.The reported total fits that scale. Spread across 77 vaults, $665,000 averages about $8,600 per vault, which points to relatively small pools drained repeatedly rather than a few large ones. It also explains why the attack could be repeated mechanically: each vault offered the same function and carried the same flaw.

Yield aggregators usually deploy vaults from a shared template, and each vault's strategy contract inherits the same logic. As a result, one unchecked function in that template turns into one exploit multiplied by every deployment. Seventy-seven vaults on five chains is what that multiplication looks like.The setup also keeps the cost of attack low. Once the flaw is understood, a script can walk through every vault on every chain, call the same function and withdraw. On top of that, ACryptoS says the stolen funds have been moved through several cross-chain protocols, a pattern that complicates recovery.

ACryptoS has asked exchanges and bridges to flag five exploiter addresses in a follow-up post on X:

The request targets exit points. With the stolen funds hopping across chains, the places where they are most likely to be cashed out or bridged are the ones best placed to slow the attacker down. These are EVM addresses and the exploit spanned five networks, so anyone investigating should check each address on Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.The rest of the response is blunt. Deposits are disabled and withdrawals remain open, with users urged to pull their assets quickly. ACryptoS cited an inability to keep maintaining the protocol, so further patching is unlikely. Remaining users should assume vault pools may be thin, withdraw while the function still works and revoke token approvals granted to ACryptoS contracts afterward. A 10% bounty is a common offer in situations like this, but whether the attacker responds is unknown, and users shouldn't plan around a recovery.

For developers, the lessons are narrow and testable. Every public function that takes an array should check its length against the data it is supposed to match. Share-minting should be tested against an invariant: the value of shares issued can never exceed the value deposited. The ERC-4626 standard defines how vault share accounting should behave, and fuzz tests built on its rules would likely have flagged this.Sunsetting a protocol needs a plan as well. A deprecated vault that still holds funds and still exposes live deposit functions is an open target. Pausing deposits and migrating balances before the maintainers leave costs little compared with leaving an unmaintained contract holding user money.For users, the story repeats a familiar warning. Small, older yield protocols with shrinking teams are the ones most likely to carry unpatched code. This incident has less to do with a clever attack than with maintenance running out before the code was safe, so the best protection is to treat vault deposits in aging projects as temporary.

Dogecoin cofounder Billy Markus shared a lighthearted observation about Japan's unique dog culture in a post on X, pointing out the popularity of Shiba Inu dogs in Japan.

"Like, 50% of the dogs I see in Japan are Shiba Inu," wrote Markus, who goes by the online handle Shibetoshi Nakamoto.

like 50% of the dogs i see in japan are shiba inu i love japan

The Dogecoin cofounder's comment is based on his own observation when he was in Japan, where the Shiba Inu breed has deep cultural roots and is still one of the country's most recognizable native dog breeds. Markus' observation is noteworthy, as he is the cofounder of Dogecoin, a cryptocurrency that draws its origins from the Shiba Inu dog.

On December 6, 2013, Dogecoin was launched, taking influence from the famous Doge meme: an image of a very adorable Shiba Inu dog with multi-colored Comic Sans text that appears as the dog's "thought bubbles."

This famous meme was based on a 2010 photograph of a Japanese female Shiba Inu dog, Kabosu, adopted by Japanese kindergarten teacher Atsuko Satō from an animal shelter in 2008. This helped establish the dog-themed cryptocurrency trend that later inspired several other tokens, including Shiba Inu (SHIB).

Kabosu, a Japanese Shiba Inu, inspired a generation of online jokes and became the face of Dogecoin cryptocurrency. Kabosu was the face of the breezy Doge meme, her quizzical expression surrounded by an inner monologue of choppy phrases in bad grammar written in rainbow-colored Comic Sans font.

In 2010, two years after adopting Kabosu from a puppy mill where she would otherwise have been put down, Ms. Satō, a teacher from Sakura, east of Tokyo, took a picture of her pet crossing her paws on the sofa. She posted the image on her blog, from where it spread to online forum Reddit and became a meme that bounced from college bedrooms to office email chains.

This inspired Dogecoin, which was started as a joke by two software engineers, Billy Markus and Jackson Palmer, and is now the 12th largest cryptocurrency, with a market capitalization of $11.17 billion, according to CoinMarketCap data.

Kabosu, the dog behind the "doge" meme, died in May 2024 after 14 years of internet fame.

#5289. Vitalik Buterin Declares Ethereum (ETH) a Store of Value, Not Fee-Burning Token

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Ethereum's intrinsic economics is rebuilding itself in motion with tech bugs and the macroeconomic picture overlaying each other in the span of 48 hours. The week wraps up for a major alternative crypto project with a sudden Glamsterdam hard fork stop after testnet launch revealed a dangerous bug in the fee recalculating mechanism, brutally breaking the logic in smart contracts.

As the Ethereum community debated the ability of the network to sustain on old power, Vitalik Buterin showed up with a manifesto which completely zeroes out all the panic around mainnet's decreasing revenue. The "red line" behind Vitalik's updated vision is that the community should stop being fixated on the idea of ETH as "fee-burninng token". For a basic blockchain layer worth $270 billion, attempts to build evaluation on the amount of gas burned are a dead end. For Vitalik, the novel of "ETH as store of value (SoV)" is much more viable amid all the global uncertainty around.

This U-turn, taken by a key visionary of the ecosystem, happened at $2,240 for ETH and may drastically change all the plans developed with a focus on Glamsterdam architecture. The hard fork was initially projected for the logic of blockspace surplus, not the deficit. Ecosystem builders are already readying expansion of L1 capacity with the help of EIP-8037 (tariffs calibration) and EIP-7928 (parallel production) with an aim to raise gas limits up to 200 million units. The logic is that the excess of free space will cheapen the transactions, while token burning rates will gradually be cut.

The market saw a risk of deflation in this concept. Vitalik took a front-step. By his estimates, the historical peaks of burning through EIP-1559 "never were as strong as they seemed". They were dependent on inner cyclical activity of crypto speculations. And it itself was falling once every bear market started.

EIP-1559 is not going anywhere, and Vitalik openly says "don't be sad" if the volume of gas burned will forever stay below the 10% mark. The source of value for Ethereum lies in completely another dimension.

Solana's co-founder, Anatoly Yakovenko, unexpectedly aligned with Buterin on this matter. "You can't focus on fees as the products", he said, calling such an idea "absolutely meaningless". According to Yakovenko, the blockchain network must generate real value for the end users, not control the price of getting into the block.

Vitalik is absolutely right that you can’t focus on fees as the product. That’s absolutely meaningless. You need to pick a product, the thing that brings value to people, and do that really well.

There is lots of technical stuff and philosophy around, but what the missed deadline on the testnet and Vitalik's manifesto reveal is that Ethereum opts for long-term, secure, and even a bit boring stability of the basic layer. Infra doesn't try to flirt with the market through deflationary records.

#5287. Flare CEO Pushes Back Against XRP 'FUD'

Flare CEO Hugo Philion has expressed his frustration about recent fear, uncertainty, and doubt (FUD) around XRP and reiterated that the future of the cryptocurrency should not be centered solely around Ripple.

The Flare CEO recently addressed in an X post the constant habit of XRP holders to evaluate the future of the cryptocurrency through the prism of what Ripple is doing and what it isn't.

"The value and narrative of XRP should never have been viewed as being dependent on the actions of a single actor," the Flare CEO said.

The Flare CEO emphasized that XRP holders should instead concentrate their efforts on finding ways to improve the usability of the cryptocurrency.

In this context, Philion said that XRP holders need to consider three main questions.

The first question is what XRP holders are actually doing to utilize their XRP holdings. The second is how they can convince potential investors to hold XRP.

Finally, the third point that the Flare CEO mentioned is that the XRP community should find a way to transform XRP from a predominantly speculative asset into usable capital.

"And that's part of the reason we created Flare because we feel like there's always been more that can and should be done with XRP," the Flare CEO added.

Besides, the Flare CEO also invited XRP holders to try Flare. According to Philion, it's a way to make XRP less dependent on Ripple.

The Flare CEO's statements come amid increasing frustration around XRP and the lackluster performance of the cryptocurrency.

Over the past year, the price of XRP has gone down by around 50%, and at press time, the price of the cryptocurrency stands at $1.16.

Recently, Ripple's former chief technology officer David Schwartz also faced some criticism over the poor performance of XRP. Schwartz noted that his influence on the XRP price was very limited.

One X user raised a question about whether FLR holders are doing enough to demonstrate the value of the cryptocurrency, especially when it's possible for XRP holders to use Flare's decentralized finance ecosystem without purchasing FLR.

Still, Philion dismissed the claim that there is no need for FLR when using FXRP (a tokenized version of XRP on Flare).

"It's incorrect btw that you can use FXRP without needing FLR," the Flare CEO clarified.

According to Philion, what Flare Smart Accounts do is simply abstract away the need to manage FLR and make the experience more convenient. At the same time, FLR is used to pay transaction fees on the underlying networks.

Besides, the Flare CEO also underlined that in the long term, there should be more use cases for the token apart from transaction fees.

"Usage is important. Need to get fee generation going in a broader way in the ecosystem," he added.

#5283. A YC startup is putting $1M behind 5 unsolved materials science problems for AI

Discovered Materials, a months-old San Francisco startup using AI models to find new substances for building advanced chips, announced a million-dollar challenge for AI models to solve five critical problems in materials science.

While frontier AI models have solved a remarkable series of outstanding mathematics problems and made progress in the life sciences, they have yet to truly plumb the complex physics in advanced materials.

“It’s more difficult to specify problems clearly in materials science because it’s not like math, where you have a very specific definition and can get to a yes or no,” said Advaith Sridhar, a co-founder of Discovered Materials, which was part of Y Combinator’s spring 2026 batch. “We came to this discussion [wondering], what are the grand challenges in this field? How do we know AI is making progress?”

Though materials science doesn’t have an equivalent of the Millennium Prize Problems, Discovered Materials recruited an advisory group of academics at leading global universities to spell out five open problems. The company is offering a pool of prizes, worth $1 million in total, for solutions to the problems.

“Across materials science, there are phenomena we observe but cannot explain,” Felipe Jornada, a Stanford professor who helped develop the challenges, said in a statement. “Explaining these phenomena would improve our understanding of physics, and the answers would directly shape how we build electronics, store energy, and manufacture the materials of the future.”

Before announcing the challenges, Discovered Materials turned frontier lab models loose on them, giving AI agents internet access and other resources to work autonomously for days. The models spent several days on each problem without making much headway. Still, it’s easy to imagine OpenAI or Anthropic attempting to one-shot them with significantly more compute or a newer model.

“It’s not particularly a concern to us whether we find it, or someone else finds it, or a professor finds it, or the frontier labs find it,” Sridhar said. “The reason we’re putting out these challenges is because we want them to serve as the goalposts. If you go and solve these challenges, we are deepening our understanding of materials and how things around us behave.”

Tracking efforts to solve the problems will show “whether the models are climbing in this domain,” he added.

The challenge also reflects the changing nature of scientific inquiry as AI proves capable of uncovering insights and techniques human researchers didn’t anticipate. With solutions apparently easier to find than ever, the questions become more important.

“This is a new way of thinking about science, where we come up with the verification and the challenges first, and then we let somebody come up with the ideas that explain the problem,” Sridhar said. “Knowing what are the right questions to ask is not trivial and very difficult in this domain, so this is where the professors have really helped us shape what are the right questions we should be asking.”

Discovered Materials’ main focus is developing new materials for use in semiconductors; the startup partners with chip giants on research projects while also funding its own scientific efforts. When the company announced its seed round in August, Sridhar told TechCrunch that he hoped the company would generate a useful material within a year.

“Those timelines have accelerated a little bit,” he says today. “I’m more confident now that we will be able to find these industrially useful materials in a timeline shorter than a year.”

#5282. Aina’s smart ring has a screen, a joystick, and a mic so you can talk to AI agents

Hardware startup Aina released a smart ring today that features a screen, a joystick, and a mic so that you can talk to your agents and take notes. The $399 ring has a speaker so you can take calls using it as well.

The startup, which raised $5.5 million in July, is positioning the ring as a controller of sorts for both AI and non-AI apps.

The company previously made Mirage, a three-key controller that let you invoke buttons based on the app on your Mac’s screen. For instance, if you were on a Google Meet call, you could map keys to camera on/off, mic mute/unmute, or to leave the meeting.

Aina has baked in lessons from that device to create the new ring, which it’s simply calling “AI ring.” Using its mic, you can take notes, send a prompt to agents, set reminders, and dictate notes on your Mac using Wispr Flow or the startup’s own dictation engine.

Now, there are already smart rings in the market that do similar things, like the Pebble Index 01, Sandbar Stream, Oasis, and Natura, which is probably why Aina has added more controls and functionality to stand out. Its ring comes with a speaker so that you can take calls, and there is a screen, which lets you see notifications from your phone or which apps you are controlling.

For navigation, there is a joystick, and it also supports gestures, so that it can trigger different actions based on what’s on your Mac or phone’s screen. The ring also lets you control music or even smart home devices like Apple TV.

I have used the ring for a few days, and it feels like a smartwatch in a ring format, with more controls. I can get notifications and reply to them. It surfaces my meetings; I can call Uber if I want to get a ride home.

It’s easier to use Apple TV’s remote itself, but the Aina ring proved useful the couple times I couldn’t find the remote. Granted, a lot of the software and features are still being fleshed out, so it’s hard to figure out where such a device ring might sit in my daily usage, but it is squarely aimed at folks who are surrounded by digital devices and AI applications.

“Phones and laptop screens were designed for an age of browsing where you think about opening apps. For interacting with proactive agents, we need a better interface, and that is what we had in mind while designing Aina,” Apoorv Shankar, Aina’s founder, told TechCrunch over a call.

Companies are trying to cater to programmers and AI enthusiasts with specialized hardware that could help them harness different agents. This includes OpenAI’s experimental keyboard and Rabbit trying to position itself as a controller. The hope with such hardware is that enough people will have multiple agents running to invest in specific gadgets to keep tabs on them.

Aina’s ring goes on preorder starting Thursday at early-bird pricing of $399, and the company plans to start shipping the device in January 2027. Once the early-bird period ends, the ring will cost $499.

#5280. Nanbeige4.3-33B Ties Qwen3.8-27B on Intelligence Index, but Spends 44% More Output Tokens

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K. Here is what that costs locally.

Two models just posted the same score. One needed 158,000 output tokens per task to get there. The other needed 110,000.

Nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5. According to Artificial Analysis's evaluation, published November 5, that matches Qwen3.8 27B at its xhigh reasoning setting. The model is open weights under Apache 2.0, accepts text only, and has a 524K-token context window.

Behind the tie sits a gap in effort. Artificial Analysis says Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task against 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more. That weighted average covers answer and reasoning tokens across all nine v5 evaluations, including agentic tool-use turns. For anyone running these models, tokens translate into time, electricity or money, so the same score doesn't mean the same cost.

The Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations, among them AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0 and AA-Omniscience. A score of 20 puts Nanbeige well above the 6 of Muse Glimmer, a 30B model in the same comparison. Artificial Analysis also notes that Nanbeige sets a new Pareto-optimal point for Intelligence Index against total parameters, since both it and Qwen3.8 27B are dense models. A larger mixture-of-experts model like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, by contrast, scores 33 while activating only 16B parameters per token.

The model card Nanbeige's lab published on Hugging Face describes the base model, positioned as the flagship teacher for the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab says it will distill agentic capabilities into smaller models, such as an upcoming 3B version. On base-model benchmarks, the card shows 66.9 on MMLU-Pro against 59.3 for Gemma4-31B-Base. Those figures belong to the base model and are separate from the reasoning model's Intelligence Index result.

The two models reach 20 by different routes. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 6% for Qwen, and 16% on the CritPt v2 Hard Subset against 4%. It also edges Qwen on AutomationBench-AA, 53% to 48%.

Elsewhere, it falls behind. On AA-Briefcase v1.1 it scores 1162 Elo against 1391, on FrontierCode 2.0 11% against 15%, and on HLE-Diamond 7% against 15%. The knowledge test tells the most distinctive story. On AA-Omniscience v1.1, Nanbeige scores -4 against Qwen's -6, with an 18% hallucination rate against 29%. Yet it answers only 29% of questions against 43%, declines 71% of them and gets 12% correct against 17%.

For general question answering, Qwen's higher accuracy is the better result.

Output tokens aren't a vanity metric. A reasoning model writes out its thinking as tokens, and every one costs decode time. If both models ran at the same speed on the same hardware, Nanbeige would take about 44% longer to finish a typical task.

Local decoding adds a second factor. Generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, because each new token requires reading the model's weights, and a 33B dense model reads about 20% more weight data per token than a 27B dense model. Assuming the same quantization and the same memory-bound hardware, those two effects compound to roughly 1.7 times the wall-clock time per task. That figure is a back-of-the-envelope calculation, not a measured result.

Nor is there a hosted alternative to soften the blow. Artificial Analysis lists no confirmed public first-party or third-party APIs for Nanbeige, so unlike Qwen, which is sold per token through Alibaba's API, the cost is the hardware you run it on and the time it takes.

Artificial Analysis describes the model as small enough to run locally on a laptop, which holds true with a caveat. The weights are published in BF16, which at 33 billion parameters means roughly 66 GB, far beyond almost any laptop. At 8-bit, the weights fall to about 33 GB, and at 4-bit to about 17 GB, plus memory for the context cache. A machine with 24 GB of unified memory or more can plausibly hold a 4-bit build, though a long context will push it.

The vendor's own quickstart points the other way. The card's SGLang and vLLM examples both set tensor parallelism across four GPUs, which suggests the reference deployment is a multi-GPU server. Its Transformers example also enables trust_remote_code=True, which runs code from the repository. Reading that code first is the safer move, as is serving the model through vLLM or SGLang instead.

Quantization changes the model, too. The Intelligence Index numbers come from Artificial Analysis's own runs, so a 4-bit local build may score somewhat lower, or generate different token counts, than the version they evaluated.

This release is a clean example of why a headline score isn't enough. Nanbeige delivers Qwen-level results at 33B, with strengths in terminal tasks and physics reasoning and a more cautious answering style. The price for those strengths is length.

Anyone choosing between the two should run both on their own workload and record three numbers: the score on their tasks, output tokens per task and seconds per task on their hardware. For terminal-heavy, agentic work, Nanbeige's profile may justify the longer runs. For knowledge-heavy or latency-sensitive work, Qwen's shorter, more accurate answers look stronger.

Three signals are worth watching next: whether the 3B distilled version keeps the model's strengths, whether other labs report the same token behavior, and whether anyone publishes quantized local benchmarks. Until then, the simplest summary is also the most accurate: same score, different bill.

#5278. Zipline hits $21.5B valuation as Walmart expands bet on drone delivery

Zipline has raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart, a pair of deals that have raised the autonomous drone delivery and logistics startup’s profile and valuation.

Zipline and Walmart reached a new multi-year agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States. The two companies have had a drone delivery agreement since 2021, but this deal is a significant jump from the 21 active drone delivery sites they have together today.

On the fundraising side, Zipline’s $1.5 billion raise was led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, with participation from Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Uber, Tiger Global, J.P. Morgan, ARK Invest, and Salesforce Ventures. Zipline is now valued at $21.5 billion.

The company, which has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software, said it plans to use the funds to expand its U.S. manufacturing facilities and hire more workers to build out a nationwide drone delivery network.

Founded in 2014, Zipline got its start in Africa, where it used its autonomous drones to deliver blood in Rwanda, and later expanded to Ghana and Nigeria. The California-based company began its first operations in the U.S. in 2020, ferrying medical equipment and supplies to Novant Health in North Carolina. The following year, it struck a deal with Walmart.

But it was in 2022 that Zipline’s business really started to take off in the United States. Zipline received its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration that year, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to complete long-range commercial drone deliveries. It has locked in a number of partnerships since then, including with Uber earlier this year.

Zipline now uses its drones to deliver food, retail, agricultural, and health products in five African countries, several cities in the United States, and Japan. Zipline’s home delivery service uses Zipline’s Platform 2 drones, which are designed to carry up to eight pounds and travel to customers within a 10-mile radius. Its larger Platform 1 drones are used for long-range deliveries for enterprise, business, and government that can cover 120 miles round trip.

The company said Thursday that its share of delivery revenue grew from 10.8% to 34.9% between March and October of this year. This latest funding aims to push that metric even higher.

#5277. Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics

It feels like AI is cracking a new math problem every week. Last month, OpenAI released 719 manuscriptsclaiming solutions to some of the field’s hardest problems. But even the computer checks meant to confirm those results can slip. After years of AI slop, it’s fair to wonder whether math is next.

Axiom Math is betting math can avoid that fate, not by slowing down, but by standing on firmer ground. The $1.6 billion startup wants to build a verified foundation that AI agents can rely on to write software and, eventually, do science.

On Wednesday, the company announced it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics ever written by humans. Mathematicians often hold Stacks in rare regard — Columbia mathematician Peter Woit has claimed there’s “nothing else really comparable,” comparing the project to “the famous Bourbaki books,” a series that rebuilt math from its foundations in the 20th century.

Woit’s Columbia colleague Johan de Jong started the Stacks Project in 2005 as an open source reference. Mathematicians have contributed to it ever since, building out results from college-level algebra all the way up to the field’s most advanced ideas across algebra, geometry, and number theory.

The company’s fleet of AI agents translates the library’s roughly 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of computer-checked code.

Formalizing math is a way of making sure the structure underneath it is sound. Mathematicians rewrite the proof as code in a programming language called Lean, and a program called a proof assistant checks the code line by line. If the proof passes, mathematicians can trust that it’s logically sound.

Engineers use the same idea, called formal verification, to confirm their chip designs work, while researchers in France have used it to catch bugs in software that calculates family benefits.

For a library like the Stacks Project, checking each theorem is only part of the job. The theorems and definitions in Stacks are interconnected, and each one builds on the ones before it. Like a family tree, many results in Stacks trace back to the ones that came before it.

That interconnectedness made Axiom unsure the project would work at first. The team had to keep every connection intact across about 16 million lines of Lean code.

“Things that are big and things that are delicate in life just don’t go together,” Axiom CEO Carina Hong told TechCrunch. “[Stacks] is a collection of mathematical results that is the foundation of mathematics. You want [theorems] to be consistent and not, like, paradoxical. You want the definitions to not fight with each other.”

The 25-year-old CEO dropped out of a Stanford math PhD program and founded the company in March 2025. In March, Axiom raised a $200 million Series A led by Menlo Ventures.

“We were not sure if vibe coding would be able to preserve the beauty of Stacks,” Hong said.

To pull off the project, the team gave its agents a loose structure and let them run in parallel. “With Stacks, we imposed a hierarchy … [but] it was not, like, a complete hierarchy of dictating what every single agent was doing,” said Ashvin Swaminathan, a member of Axiom’s technical staff. “The agents were finding tasks for themselves and identified things that they could work on in parallel.”

Axiom also trained its own models to be good at math, an approach Hong said most other verification startups haven’t taken. At first, the team relied on one of its in-house Lean experts to teach the agents a human sense of taste. Over time, Hong said, the agents have picked up taste on their own.

The result fills one of the biggest gaps in formalized math. “When you look at what has been formalized in mathematics, there’s this huge black hole. And that black hole covers algebraic geometry,” Swaminathan said.

Until now, researchers who wanted to check new work in algebraic geometry with Lean had little to build on, Swaminathan said. “Well, now they do.”

Axiom argues that each verified result becomes a building block, so future proofs can lean on checked math instead of starting from scratch. Terence Tao, the UCLA mathematician and Fields Medal winner, has made the general case more simply: “The more formalized proofs you have, the more formalized proofs you can make.”

Mathematicians aren’t Axiom’s only intended audience. Developers have long struggled to guarantee that their code is free of bugs and security holes. That problem grows as AI agents write more of the world’s code.

Axiom is betting that the software of the future will need to rest on verified foundations, the way Stacks now does.

“We believe that mathematics is the domain where you start building these things and that it’s a transferable skill,” Swaminathan said. “Agents can read our code, understand it, and build new infrastructure on top of it. Our Lean formalization is now the substrate that agents can build upon.”

The way Axiom’s agents built Stacks, working in parallel and picking their own tasks, is how Hong expects much of AI’s future work to happen. AI agents, she argues, will need a well-built, reusable body of knowledge to keep from producing slop.

“You want [agents] to have a reusable library for them to build on and keep pushing the frontier,” Hong said. “If you slop drop in a way that’s bad engineering choices in the beginning, then it’s very hard for them to grow that boundary.”

Hong is confident enough in that approach to issue a dare. “I openly challenge all the coding companies to work on formalization at this scale.”

Bitcoin snapped a seven-week holding above the 50-week moving average (MA) with a weekly close at $74,968. According to the latest Galaxy Research report, BTC settled 0.7% under this key line, which now sits at $75,488.

Alex Thorn, the firm’s head of research, calls it a fakeout. The history is on his side: it's standard Bitcoin mechanics to slip back under the 50-week MA right after a bear-market bottom, and it's what shapes the structure of the four-year cycle. It has happened exactly twice before.

Losing the trendline again right after reclaiming it is how the biggest cryptocurrency has always behaved. Previous cycles played out like this:

The current chart is running the same script. From the $123,524 peak in October 2025, the coin bled 51.8% into the June cycle bottom at $59,517. A rebound then shoved the price back above the 50-week MA at $81,195. Today’s price is 7.7% off that September reclaim level, yet Bitcoin maintains a comfortable 26% cushion above the June bottom.

Thorn isn’t selling certainty. Two cycles is a thin sample, and bottoms only get confirmed in the rearview mirror. The margin for error is wide: in 2012, Bitcoin broke down again from 18% above the line, while in 2015 it held from just 8% above.

“Bitcoin just closed below its 50 week moving average after holding above it for 7 consecutive weeks. Two other times (2011-12 & 2019-20) btc closed below its 50w after reclaiming its post-bear bottom. Neither of those times did the bear make a new lower low (weekly close data),” the analyst notes.

One level kills the bull case for this 4-year cycle: $59,517. Galaxy Research says on-chain metrics, whale positioning and market sentiment all point to a consolidation that is technically ripe for stacking on spot. The technical case stays alive as long as Bitcoin reclaims the 50-week MA and holds it within the next month.

#5269. Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

SlowMist says five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit. Here is how the check failed.Every one of the five receipts was signed by the bridge's own trusted signer. Every one pointed to a deposit that had already been paid out.

On November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge. According to SlowMist's alert, the attacker built five forged receipts that all referenced a single legitimate Optimism transaction, changing the recipient, the token and the withdrawal amount in each one.

All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.

The reused transaction was tiny: a deposit of about 0.0044 ankrETH made on Optimism on November 3, which SlowMist's analysis says had already been redeemed on Ethereum the same day. Six days later, that one settled deposit was cited five times. The incident is recorded in the SlowMist Hacked database.Blockaid flagged the exploit as it unfolded, at about 08:42 UTC, with roughly $292,000 already gone. SlowMist followed at 09:14 UTC with the higher $304,500 estimate and an explanation of the forged receipts. Ankr paused withdrawals, and no recovery plan has been confirmed.

The design is common across lock-and-release bridges. A user deposits on the source chain, and an off-chain set of signers watches for that deposit and signs a receipt describing it. The destination contract, in this case Ankr's Ethereum bridge contract, checks that the receipt carries a valid signature and then releases the funds.That setup makes the signers the source of truth. The contract can't see Optimism, so it leans on the signature to prove the deposit happened. The weak point sits in the gap between "the signer signed this" and "this really happened." A contract that treats the first as proof of the second inherits every mistake the signing process makes.

SlowMist's finding is precise: the withdrawal function released assets without independently verifying the actual event on the source chain. A signature confirmed that the signer approved a message. It did not confirm that the message matched a deposit that existed, that was still unused, and that involved the same recipient, token and amount.The replay angle deserves attention, even though SlowMist's summary only implies it. A bridge normally marks each source event as consumed, keyed to something fixed like the source chain, transaction hash and log index, so it can be paid out once. If replay protection keys on the contents of the receipt instead, changing the recipient, token or amount produces a receipt the contract has never seen. Five edited receipts against one deposit would then look like five fresh claims. That is one plausible way the pieces fit together, not a finding the researchers have published.Bridge history offers parallels. In 2022, Wormhole lost about $325 million when an attacker got a forged message past its signature verification, and Nomad lost about $190 million after a misconfiguration let nearly any message pass as valid. The Ankr case is smaller, but it shares the same root: the verification step accepted something it shouldn't have.

The Ethereum transactions show the attacker extracted about 82.91 ankrETH, 515,206 ankrPOL and 7.98 million ANKR tokens. Blockaid described the five withdraw calls as using the tiny Optimism deposit to unlock the bridge's locked inventory and send it to a new wallet.The mix of assets tells its own story. Each forged receipt named a different token and amount, which suggests the attacker picked targets based on what the bridge held. That fits receipts built entirely by the attacker, apart from the one real transaction reference. Anyone wanting to trace them can open the bridge contract's transaction list on Etherscan and filter for the five `withdraw` calls on November 9.

The most important fact is still missing. SlowMist says the origin of the unauthorized signatures is under investigation, and it hasn't confirmed whether the signers were compromised.A valid signature on a forged receipt has a short list of explanations. A signing key, or the service holding it, could have been accessed. A signing service could have been tricked into signing attacker-supplied data. Or the signing logic itself could have a flaw that produces signatures for receipts it shouldn't. Each one points to a different fix: a stolen key means rotating signers, a manipulated service means tightening input validation off-chain, and a logic flaw means rewriting the signing rules.Whichever it turns out to be, the on-chain contract and the off-chain signer both failed to ask the same question. Either one verifying the source event would likely have stopped the attack, and neither did.

The lessons are narrow and practical. Replay protection should key on the immutable identity of the source event, not on the receipt's contents, and a source event should be consumable exactly once. The destination contract should confirm that the receipt's recipient, token and amount match what the source-chain event actually recorded, using a proof or an independent verifier instead of trusting the signer alone.Signer infrastructure needs its own scrutiny. Threshold schemes, hardware-backed keys and strict limits on what a signing service will sign all shrink the damage from a single failure. Rate limits and per-withdrawal caps help as well. A bridge that can release its entire locked inventory in five calls has no brake once a signature check is defeated.Trust in a bridge comes in layers, and one layer rarely holds up alone. Users with funds in Ankr's bridge should watch for the project's post-mortem and its plan for restoring withdrawals. For developers, the question to put to their own code is a blunt one: if a signer signs something false, what stops the contract from believing it?

#5268. 'I Sold 2.5 Million XRP': Ripple Vet David Schwartz Rebuts Critics With Tax Proof

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. XRP Ledger co-creator David Schwartz dropped his $1.7 million tax bill on X to settle a long-running fight over the token’s value. Ripple’s CTO Emeritus was swatting away haters who accused him of dumping XRP on the market. One commenter called XRP “a terrible investment,” adding that nobody would blame the engineer for heading for the exit. Schwartz kept it short: “The $1.7 million I paid in capital gains tax says otherwise.”

In 2025, Schwartz sold about 2.5 million XRP, according to his own words. Nearly all of it came from bonuses for his work in 2020 and 2023. Posting the numbers was no accident. Schwartz is killing rumors about what Ripple’s "big guns" really pocket and proving he has nothing to hide.

The sale is one chapter in a bigger personal saga Schwartz has been unpacking piece by piece from 2024 through 2026. At his peak he held around 26 million XRP. By August 2026, that stack had shrunk to just 2 million. Describing the 92% drawdown, he chose his words carefully: “I think I’m down from about 26 million at my peak to about 2 million now.”

Some went out as gifts and transfers, but he sold most of it on the open market.

He started taking profits the moment the price touched $0.10. Schwartz admits he never believed the coin would break $0.25. The same paranoia made him dump his entire 40,000 ETH position at a measly $1.05 apiece.

“Obviously, I wish I hadn’t done those things,” the developer says of the billions he left on the table.

Schwartz opposes the approach many attribute to as "diamond hands". He openly says he “really, really hates risk” and doesn’t count himself among long-term holders. He and his wife had an ironclad rule to sell a fixed slice of their holdings every time the price printed a new all-time high. Cashing out is simply the cost of being able to “sleep better at night.” These days, volatility barely touches him as his net worth is now largely cut loose from price swings.

Based on his own admission, Schwartz moved most of his savings into Ripple stock. The shares are illiquid, sure, but they give direct exposure to the tech giant’s wins and fully insulate his personal capital from exchange chaos.

Zcash has set a new high in its network hashrate just days after the NU7 upgrade, which slashed block times by a third to 25 seconds. Zcash activated its NU7 upgrade on November 6, 2026, at block 3,543,405.

Zcash network hashrate: 32.62 GSol/s, up 5.8% in 30 days. ⛏️ An all-time high. https://t.co/1vNROBAvd2

Zcash hashrate refers to the total computing power of all miners on the ZEC network. It is calculated by the current network difficulty, the average block find time set by the cryptocurrency network and/or the effective block find time of the latest blocks.

ZEC got 3x faster following the NU7 upgrade, which launched on November 6, with block times down from 75 to 25 seconds, and the Sprout pool retired, marking a new era for Zcash.

Faster blocks mean more room for shielded transactions. NU7 adds per-block limits: 330 Orchard or Ironwood actions, 300 Sapling inputs and outputs, a shared budget of 330 across pools, and no new Sprout JoinSplits. These limits more than double Orchard protocol throughput while reducing the worst-case sync load a spammer can push onto light wallets by about 37%.

NU7 does not raise Zcash's fixed 21 million cap; halvings will now come every 5,040,000 blocks instead of 1,680,000, so the issuance schedule holds at roughly four years per halving. NU7 also starts allocating funds for future mining rewards. Some 60% of aggregate transaction fees will flow into a public reserve that pays later mining rewards.

In what comes next after the NU7 upgrade, Zcash developers have proposed cutting block times in a potential NU7.1 upgrade just days after NU7 went live. The proposal would reduce target block times from 25 to 20 seconds, aiming to speed up transaction confirmations and improve user experience and network latency.

#5265. After challenging Google’s Android with Cyanogen, its co-founder takes aim at Windows for AI era

Almost a decade after Cyanogen shut down its Android operating-system business following a years-long, unsuccessful effort to loosen Google’s dominance, its co-founder, Kirt McMaster, is now targeting Microsoft’s Windows with a new operating system designed for people who rely heavily on artificial intelligence in their everyday work.

McMaster’s company, Kora Systems, on Tuesday unveiled a Linux-based desktop operating system that integrates AI models and autonomous agents directly into the computing experience, allowing them to work across applications, access files, and retain context between tasks. The software is expected to launch in 2027 as a free-to-use desktop operating system, with support for existing Intel- and AMD-powered PCs as well as machines running Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips.

Kora is developing the eponymous operating system with a team of about 50 engineers, relying on AI coding tools, including OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude. McMaster told TechCrunch that these tools have accelerated development by at least fivefold, with most of the gains coming over the past six months.

Microsoft has long dominated the PC operating-system market, making it hard for newer players to establish a foothold. Windows held about 77% of the worldwide desktop operating-system market in October, compared with nearly 10% for Apple’s OS X, according to Statcounter’s web traffic data.

However, McMaster believes Kora does not need to compete for Windows’ entire user base. Rather, he is targeting people who use AI extensively and are willing to pay for access to powerful models and services.

“Microsoft can keep its billion users,” McMaster said, estimating that 45 million to 50 million people currently account for much of AI usage and revenue. He expects that market to exceed 200 million users by 2033.

McMaster told TechCrunch that his experience at Cyanogen, where he spent over five years, taught him the dangers of relying on the very company he was trying to challenge. Cyanogen remained heavily dependent on Google Mobile Services despite offering features beyond Google’s version of Android. That ultimately restricted its ability to build an independent ecosystem.

“If you are trying to compete with an incumbent but are still reliant on them, you have no chance,” he said.

Kora, McMaster said, builds on an idea he pursued toward the end of his time at Cyanogen, when he began exploring ways to integrate third-party services directly into the operating system. With Kora, he wants AI models and agents to work across applications and access files without being confined to individual apps.

Previously known as Playtron, a gaming operating-system company led by McMaster, the Palo Alto-based company rebranded as Kora in July 2025 as it shifted its focus to AI. The decision came as early companies, including Perplexity and OpenAI, were moving into AI-powered web browsers, McMaster said. He believed browsers would not give AI agents enough access to a computer to carry out more complex tasks, making an operating system a better starting point.

The shift also allowed Kora to build on nearly three years of work developing Playtron’s Linux-based gaming operating system, called GameOS, instead of starting from scratch.

Kora is designed to let users work with different AI models and agents across applications, while keeping track of conversations, documents, and other information. It also allows AI agents to operate in separate workspaces with restricted access to files and other resources.

While McMaster has drawn on his experience at Cyanogen, none of Kora’s engineers worked there. Instead, the company recruited heavily from the Linux gaming community, he told TechCrunch.

Kora’s software is built on Linux and uses Nix. It replaces the Fedora Silverblue foundation of Playtron’s earlier GameOS.

While Linux and Nix are open source, McMaster said Kora’s own technology, including its Cortex AI engine and desktop interface, remains proprietary. The company, he said, intends to support AI models and services from different providers, although it has not committed to making its own software open source.

Gaming also remains part of Kora’s plans. McMaster said the company intends to introduce AI-powered tools that would allow developers to create, publish, and play games directly within the operating system. He added that support for Android apps is also on its roadmap.

McMaster told TechCrunch that Kora’s team has worked closely with Qualcomm’s engineers for nearly a year to optimize the operating system specifically for Snapdragon-powered PCs. The collaboration includes support for Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite chips.

Alongside Qualcomm, Kora is working with Saudi Arabia’s AI company Humain on an enterprise version of the operating system, called Humain OS, which is expected to run on Snapdragon-powered laptops in 2027. Kora also plans to announce partnerships with PC manufacturers at a later date, though McMaster did not identify any companies or provide a specific timeline.

Kora plans to generate revenue through subscriptions that bundle access to AI models and agentic services. Moreover, its Cortex engine is designed to run AI tasks locally when possible and use cloud-based models for work requiring more computing power.

Kora’s investors include Samsung Next, Square Enix, Alumni Ventures, Polychain, VanEck, and Circle, all of which previously backed Playtron. The company, McMaster said, has raised additional funding since shifting its focus to AI. However, he declined to disclose the total amount raised or its valuation. Kora has enough funding to operate for several years, he said.

#5264. Ethereum (ETH) Gas Estimates Are Broken: Explaining the Fix and the Issue

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Ethereum transactions can appear successful, but there might be a problem hiding behind the scenes.

A Geth developer has proposed a fix to the client's gas estimation, according to draft pull request #36084 on GitHub. The patch addresses an issue in the current estimator, which could result in incorrect gas limits due to failed internal calls (calls from one smart contract to another) being ignored.

Although the transaction could still be completed, there is no evidence that the action the user wanted has actually happened.

The issue lies in a mechanism where a smart contract calls another smart contract, catches an error, and then proceeds to a refund, records the failure, or skips an item entirely. Technically, the transaction was successful, but the outcome is different for the user.

This could potentially result in wallets suggesting a gas limit that is enough to finish the transaction, but not enough to complete the work inside it. The developer also noted that EIP-8037 could make this behavior more common, since gas returned from failed internal execution can help fund the fallback.

According to the pull request, the change includes a stricter definition of success for gas estimates. This version of Geth would improve the way it deals with internal failures, counting failed internal calls and contract creations instead of checking only whether the transaction completes.

Even if the transaction completes, the estimate would get rejected if it produces more internal failures than a reference execution with a higher gas limit.

Nonetheless, the developer stressed that an internal call that always fails should not push the estimate higher indefinitely. The reference execution enables the estimator to keep existing failures without allowing additional ones caused by insufficient gas. The proposal also introduces a separate Amsterdam reference, preventing unnecessary increases made purely to access the state gas reservoir.

The developer states that they've replayed 432 mainnet transactions with the new set of rules from the Amsterdam update and that the suggested change fixed 64 out of 67 cases.

The gas limit increased by 4%. 254 additional estimates were unaffected due to the lack of the problem, with 3 cases being undetected.

For regular investors, the proposed change should improve the reliability of wallet estimates and reduce transactions that complete without delivering the intended result, despite introducing higher gas limits in some cases. Luckily, there is no proven link between higher gas limits and higher fees.

Cardano (ADA) has entered epoch 666, yet another milestone for the blockchain, which has been live since its launch in September 2017.

The number has drawn attention for its connection to the biblical 666, but the development also points to the Cardano network's basic timekeeping and staking mechanism.

Popular Cardano blockchain explorer Cexplorer displays that epoch 666 started on Nov. 5, 2026, and is expected to end on Nov. 10, with 1 day and 10 hours left to close. The milestone marks another five-day cycle finished in Cardano's long-running proof-of-stake system.

Cardano divides its operation into epochs, which are five days long and consist of 432,000 one-second slots. The importance of epoch 666 is largely symbolic and not technical, as it does not coincide with any major protocol upgrades or hard forks. But the number 666 has merely provided an interesting talking point for the Cardano community.

In a separate milestone, the Cardano network has processed over 127,000,000 transactions on mainnet. According to Cexplorer data, Cardano has recorded a total of 127,203,164 transactions.

In upgrade news, DijkstraNet, the Dijkstra hard fork testnet, has been hard forked to protocol version 12 and is now available for testing and integration against the full Dijkstra feature set, with the exception of Linear Leios.

Node 11.2 was pre-released on October 28 and successfully used to transition DijkstraNet into the Dijkstra era, and DB Sync 13.8.0.0 was released for all networks.

In separate upgrade news, Midnight has completed its upgrade from Ledger 8 to Ledger 9, bringing new capabilities for developers alongside security, compatibility, and performance improvements across the network.

Ledger 9 introduces native support for widely used cryptographic standards including ECDSA and Keccak-256, expands wallet and custody compatibility, and enables contracts to interact directly with one another.

Keccak-256 is the standard algorithm that Ethereum uses to scramble data into fixed-length cryptographic fingerprints. ECDSA is the standard digital signature method that networks like Bitcoin and Ethereum use to prove ownership of a specific wallet address.

#5259. How Bittensor's Gamma Turns Every AI Payment Into an Alpha Burn

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token. Here is how gamma gets minted, how the lower-price rule works and why the credit can never be converted back.Pay a Bittensor subnet for an AI answer with gamma, and your payment vanishes. The alpha token behind it gets burned, the credit gets spent, and nobody can redeem either one.

Using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine. Opentensor announced gamma to cut that friction. With gamma, a Bittensor wallet handles both access and payment across any subnet that adopts the standard.The mechanics are laid out in the gamma guide in the subtensor docs. Gamma is a credit a subnet can accept as payment, valued in US dollars. A customer gets it by burning that subnet's alpha token, and each dollar of burned alpha value mints one gamma, so a burn valued at $100 creates 100 gamma.Each balance stays tied to the subnet where it was created. Gamma minted for subnet 51 can't pay for a service on any other subnet. Root switches the system on network-wide, and each subnet owner or lease beneficiary then enables it for their own subnet.

Customers have two ways in. They can pay with TAO, and the protocol buys the subnet’s alpha and burns it in a single transaction. Or they can pay with alpha they already hold on that subnet, and the protocol burns it directly to create gamma.

Setup takes four steps. The customer creates a fresh hotkey that will act as an API key, associates it with their coldkey, looks up the service they want and mints. The docs give the command: btcli gamma mint --netuid 51 --hotkey API_KEY --amount-tao 10 --service-hotkey SERVICE_HOTKEY. The TAO route follows the same pool and flow accounting as stake-burn and creates no stake position. Users who hold stake can burn it with mint-gamma-with-stake, and --amount-alpha all burns the whole position.

The gamma lands in a deposit. Each deposit belongs to the minting coldkey and is keyed by the API-key hotkey, which signs the customer's requests. A hotkey holds at most one deposit per subnet, and a coldkey holds at most 64 per subnet. The docs warn against reusing a staking hotkey or a coldkey, because requests signed with the key get paid from the deposit.A few guardrails apply. A mint must reach at least 0.1 gamma. By default, the SDK quotes the mint first and fails it if the result lands more than 5% below the quote. The mint also needs a TAO/USD price no older than 300 blocks, about an hour.

Gamma’s valuation rule decides how much credit a burn buys. The protocol values the burned alpha in TAO, then converts that figure to dollars through an on-chain TAO/USD price feed. The TAO value equals alpha multiplied by the lower of two prices, the gamma price and the spot price, which the docs write as alpha × min(gamma price, spot price).

Every subnet keeps a gamma price. When a subnet registers, the price starts at the median alpha price across subnets. After that it moves asymmetrically. If spot falls, the gamma price falls to match at once. If spot rises, the gamma price climbs slowly toward it, closing a small slice of the gap each block, so the gap halves every 600 blocks, roughly two hours. However high spot jumps, the gamma price can at most double every 600 blocks.An example shows the effect. Say a user burns 100 alpha when spot sits at 0.05 TAO but the gamma price lags at 0.04. The mint uses 0.04, which gives 4 TAO of value, and at $400 per TAO that mints 1,600 gamma. Had the gamma price caught up, the same burn would mint 2,000, so the lag costs the burner 400 gamma. A short-lived pump buys no extra credit. The figures are illustrative, but the rule comes straight from the docs.The TAO/USD feed gets similar damping. A root-controlled oracle supplies the price, and the accepted price falls to a lower feed immediately but rises at most 66 parts per million per block, about 2% an hour. The docs admit the oracle is trusted: its accepted price can climb up to roughly 61% a day until root replaces or removes it.One more detail matters. The docs say alpha is valued at these prices, not at what selling it would return, so a burn that is large relative to the pool is worth more than a sale would be. A big burner gets credit for full value instead of a slipped sale price.Once minted, gamma holds its dollar value whether TAO or alpha prices rise or fall. Service providers still set their own prices.

To use a service, a person or an AI agent signs a request with a hotkey from their Bittensor wallet. The subnet owner, or another authorized account, deducts the required credits from that hotkey's gamma balance before delivering the service. Nothing transfers to anyone. The designated spender calls `spend-gamma` with up to 512 entries per call, each naming a hotkey, an amount and a 32-byte reference, and the spent gamma is destroyed on the spot.The reference doubles as a receipt. By convention it holds the service's own ID for the request being paid, returned with the response, so the customer can match each spend to a specific request. The chain repeats the reference in its events and reads it nowhere else, so an entry sent twice spends twice.Customers keep control throughout. The minting coldkey can set a daily spend cap that refills linearly over 7,200 blocks, about a day, and a cap of zero pauses the deposit. The coldkey can also change the spender, keep separate deposits for different apps and agents, and top up an existing deposit without switching hotkeys. Because the coldkey can pause or redirect at any moment, services spend ahead: they spend what they are about to serve, then serve what was spent. A spender can hand this right to a `GammaSpend` proxy, which can make no other call.Both minting and spending leave public records on-chain, so anyone can audit how much credit a subnet has created and how much customers have used.

The limits are strict. Gamma can't be transferred to another wallet, and it can't be converted back into alpha or TAO. It confers no claim on any party and can't be redeemed. Each subnet chooses whether, and at what prices, it accepts its own gamma.

The docs flag the sharpest risk directly: dissolving or pruning a subnet destroys all of its gamma, and holders receive nothing. A customer who prepaid a large deposit to a subnet that later shuts down loses it. Moving gamma between your own deposits is allowed, and a deposit opened under someone else's hotkey stays yours, since you can pull the gamma back at any time.A coldkey swap adds a few wrinkles. While one is announced, the coldkey's gamma calls are refused, though its spenders keep spending. After a subnet owner swaps coldkeys, deposits that name the old one keep it until the owner republishes its service.

The docs answer the economic question in one sentence: spent gamma pays its spender nothing. The value of the burned alpha accrues to the subnet's alpha holders.

That makes gamma a direct demand mechanism for alpha. Creating gamma always burns the subnet's alpha, which removes those tokens from circulation for good. When customers pay with TAO, the protocol first buys alpha from the subnet's pool, so TAO-funded purchases add buying pressure before the burn. Every dollar of AI usage ties a purchase of service credits to a burn of alpha.

A service operator earns through the alpha it holds and the emissions its subnet receives, not through a payment from customers. The structure rewards subnets that attract real usage, since usage shrinks their alpha supply.Two questions remain open. Customers get dollar-denominated credit, but the burn that funds it follows alpha prices, so heavy usage during a price spike may feel expensive. Holders also carry the dissolution risk, which will push careful buyers toward established subnets. Which services accept gamma, and at what price, will show whether this becomes a real payments layer or a niche tool. The mechanism is clear, and adoption is the unknown.

#5258. Bitcoin Price Falls Ahead of Jobs Report: Is a Fourth Sell-Off Inbound?

Bitcoin news: BTC closed below its 200-day EMA before the jobs report. It rose after 52 of 104 reports, but fell after the last 3.

In Bitcoin news on Friday, November 6, BTC heads into the US October jobs report at 8:30 a.m. ET after closing Thursday at $76,088. BTC USD price is now below its 200-day average for the first time since August 19.

The report itself has been a coin toss. The recent record has not.

Payroll employment rises by 165,000 in October; unemployment rate changes little at 4.1% https://t.co/ZwrVfLvQgj #JobsReport #BLSdata

— BLS-Labor Statistics (@BLS_gov) November 6, 2026

A Coinspeaker review of all 104 jobs reports since January 2018 shows Bitcoin was higher 24 hours later after exactly 52 of them. A week later, though, it was lower after each of the last three: down 3.3% in August, 5.2% in September and 3.7% in October.

The setup is already weak. Bitcoin trades at $76,160, down 5.1% in 24 hours, after Thursday’s chip-stock sell-off dragged it from $80,918 to $75,208, its lowest since September 16. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index fell from 50 to 28 in a day.

The jobs data also feeds straight into the Fed. Traders on Polymarket now price a 69% chance of a rate hike on December 9, down from 80% a day earlier.

So what does Bitcoin usually do after a jobs report, and can it win back the 200-day line?

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Best Low-Cap Crypto

Not much to bet on the first day. The direction only starts to lean after a week, and only slightly.

We measured BTC from the hourly candle of each 8:30 a.m. ET release on Binance, using the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ release archive for the dates. The October 2025 report, never published because of the government shutdown, is not included.

This year broke into two halves. Bitcoin was higher a week after each of 2026’s first seven jobs reports, by 0.5% to 7.6%. Then it fell after all three since August.

One caveat: a week leaves room for other news to take over. The worst 24 hours in the sample came after the December 2021 report, a 17.1% drop that came with a weekend leverage flush.

DISCOVER: Fed Meeting Today: Traders Price a 95% Hold and a 79% December Hike. What Does It Mean for Crypto?

Because the Fed is leaning toward a hike, not a cut. It held rates at 3.75% to 4% on October 28 in a 10–2 vote, and both dissenters wanted a quarter-point hike.

Thursday’s crash already cooled that bet. Kalshi’s odds of a December hike dropped 10 points in a day, while a hold rose from 22% to 32%.

A strong report would likely push hike odds back up. A weak one would give the Fed room to wait, and with it, one less reason for traders to sell risk.

DISCOVER: Bitcoin Holds $79,200 Before the Fed, Coinbase Earnings and a $10.9B Expiry: Which Way Next?

Not yet. BTC sits about $380 under its 200-day exponential moving average (EMA) at $76,540, a line it had held on every daily close since its August breakout.

The jobs report has rarely set Bitcoin’s direction on the day. For traders following Bitcoin news this week, the weekly close against the 200-day EMA will matter more than the payroll number.
