#5168. Binance hack funds worth $430K traced through 6 NEAR memecoins – Report

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

The tremors of the Binance exploit are still being felt, as, according to a recent report by Elliptic, the North Korean hackers are using a new method to launder stolen cryptocurrency by creating their own worthless meme tokens.

Instead of transferring stolen funds directly between wallets, they are routing them through decentralized exchange (DEX) liquidity pools. This is done to make it harder and more time-consuming for investigators to trace where the money goes.

This time, the hacker started by creating a new cryptocurrency token using publicly available token-launch platforms. Soon after that, they paired this token with a legitimate asset, such as Near Protocol [NEAR] or a stablecoin, in a liquidity pool on a DEX.

Providing more insights on the matter, the report added,

Each of the six NEAR tokens carries a logo in classic meme coin style…The names follow meme coin habits too, from a crude joke (FUK) to an echo of the “-INU” dog coins (SINU).

They then used wallets holding stolen funds to buy the newly created token.

Finally, another set of wallets sold those tokens back into the same pool and withdrew legitimate crypto assets. Now since the liquidity pool sat between the buying and selling wallets, there was no direct transfer of stolen funds between them.

According to this blockchain analytics firm, this technique was previously observed during the laundering of funds stolen from the Bybit hack in 2025.

At that time, too, the wrongdoers had moved at least $24 million through a worthless token created on the Tron [TRON] network.

The same approach has now appeared as Elliptic identified its use across TRON [TRX], NEAR, and Solana [SOL]. In fact, between 5th and 7th November, hackers created at least six memecoins on NEAR, including FUK, OLCCL, MEILI, MMLI, DABI, and SINU, with each token costing approximately 25 NEAR, or $90.

In this, around 117,000 NEAR, worth approximately $430,000, passed through these six tokens. The transactions followed a similar pattern, with tokens experiencing heavy trading within hours of creation before being abandoned. In some cases, the remaining liquidity was also withdrawn.

This followed the FBI attributing the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group. All this while, North Korean cyber-espionage group Kimsuky is increasingly using AI tools to strengthen its cyberattacks.

#5167. Arca Opens to Everyone, Paying People for the AI Sessions They’d Otherwise Throw Away

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

After invite-only early access, the desktop app from the team behind Brevis is now open to anyone on Mac and Windows.

HONG KONG, November 11, 2026: Arca, a new desktop app from the team behind Brevis, opened to the public today. Arca pays people for the AI sessions they’d otherwise throw away. It finds the session history their AI tools already keep on their computer, lets them choose which sessions to submit, strips sensitive details on the device before anything is uploaded, and pays for the sessions that are approved. Starting today, anyone can sign up with an email address, with no invite and no waitlist.

Much of today’s knowledge work runs through AI tools. People steer a model through a task, correcting it, throwing out what fails and keeping what holds up. Every one of those sessions leaves a detailed record of real work: the back-and-forth, the dead ends, the fix that finally worked. These records pile up by the thousands on people’s computers, and once the window closes, they’re worth nothing to the person who did the work. Arca gives that work a value.

Arca works with the AI tools people already use, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Claude Desktop. After installing the app, users see the sessions Arca has found on their machine, past ones included. They pick a session to upload, and Arca anonymises it on their computer before it leaves, then returns a quote range. Users either confirm, which sends the session to review, or withdraw, in which case the upload is deleted. Approved sessions are paid weekly.

Arca only reads sessions that are already on the user’s computer, and it lists everything it finds. Nothing uploads in the background, and nothing leaves the device until the user picks a session and confirms. Before a session is uploaded, Arca strips names, file paths, account details and keys, and further anonymising runs on Arca’s side.

“Every AI session is a record of real thinking and real work, and until now the person who did that work got nothing for it,” said Michael, co-founder and CEO of Brevis. “Arca lets people see what their sessions are worth and decide for themselves what to share. We opened it in small batches first to get the experience right. Today it’s open to everyone.”

Arca is built for anyone who does real work with AI, from code to contract reviews, research and long working conversations. Sessions with Claude Opus and Fable, and with the latest GPT models in Codex, qualify today, with more to come. Very short sessions don’t qualify, and every submission is reviewed before it pays. Users can connect GitHub to strengthen their profile, which can raise the value of their sessions, but it isn’t required.

Arca carries the principle behind Brevis’s verifiable computing work into a new domain: things you can verify are worth more than things you have to trust.

Arca first opened on October 13 in invite-only early access, admitting users in small batches. With today’s launch, the invite requirement is gone. Users sign up with an email address or a Google account and can start right away. Arca is free to use and available now for Mac and Windows at arca.market.

Through November 30, the Arca Launch Challenge adds $10,000 in prizes on top of regular payouts for approved sessions.

Arca pays people for the AI sessions they’d otherwise throw away. The desktop app finds the sessions people’s AI tools already keep, lets them choose what to share, anonymises sessions on the device before upload, and pays for approved sessions. Arca is built by the team behind Brevis. Learn more at arca.market.

#5166. Rothschild Investment Reveals XRP ETF Stake

Rothschild Investment LLC, the Chicago-based investment management firm, has filed its latest 13F with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), revealing its stake in the Bitwise XRP ETF.

Rothschild Investment’s filing, made on Nov. 10, indicates that the company has invested in 6,300 shares of the Bitwise XRP ETF.

Based on the information provided, these shares were worth $104,769 as of Sept. 30.

The investment in the Bitwise XRP ETF is listed under CUSIP 09174F107 in Rothschild Investment’s third-quarter report.

Interestingly, Rothschild Investment did not have any reported holdings of the XRP ETF in its previous quarterly filing, which indicates that the firm’s investment in the XRP ETF occurred in the third quarter of 2026.

The Bitwise XRP ETF, listed under the ticker XRP, was introduced in November 2025.

The ETF enables traditional investors to invest in the Ripple-linked cryptocurrency without needing to buy and hold XRP tokens themselves.

Although Rothschild Investment has invested in the XRP ETF, it is not a significant part of its overall portfolio.

The firm’s total portfolio value for 13F-reportable holdings is around $2.69 billion.

Rothschild Investment holds much larger stakes in Bitcoin and Ethereum investments.

When it comes to cryptocurrencies, Rothschild Investment’s largest holding is in the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF by BlackRock, where the company owns 40,188 shares worth around $1.9 million.

Additionally, Rothschild Investment reported holding $911,300 in the Grayscale Bitcoin Trust ETF and $335,160 in the Morgan Stanley Bitcoin Trust ETF.

Other Bitcoin-related investments include the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ETF ($125,113), VanEck Bitcoin ETF ($118,100), Bitwise Bitcoin ETF ($116,802) and Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ($2,107).

In total, the seven Bitcoin investments represent around $3.51 million in reported holdings.

Rothschild Investment also has stakes in the Grayscale Ethereum Staking ETF worth $538,622 and the Bitwise Ethereum ETF worth $476,500.

The company also has a significant holding in the Bitwise Crypto Industry Innovators ETF, with 24,250 shares worth $615,223.

The firm owns $38,360 worth of shares in the Grayscale CoinDesk Crypto 5 ETF.

Finally, it has invested $69,900 in a Solana ETF.

Aside from cryptocurrency investment funds, Rothschild Investment has shares in publicly traded companies that are heavily involved in the digital asset space.

Michael Saylor’s Strategy is one such holding, with a $530,763 investment.

Other holdings include Coinbase Global ($86,681), Block ($125,060) and Riot Platforms ($42,980), a Bitcoin mining company.

#5165. Democratic Sweep Puts Crypto Bill On a Cleaner Track

Home » Regulations » Democratic Sweep Puts Crypto Bill On a Cleaner Track

Regaining the majority at the Senate has shuffled the cards for crypto legislation: will Democrats handle it better?

Democrats’ control of both chambers of Congress has raised fresh questions about how soon Washington can deliver a lasting framework for the digital asset industry.

The stalled CLARITY Act and related market-structure legislation now sit before a Congress that is expected to reopen the terms, priorities, and timing of any overhaul.

The CLARITY Act was meant to settle a core industry question: which federal regulator oversees different parts of the crypto market. Its path was already uncertain.

The new congressional balance adds further negotiation over consumer protections, disclosure rules, clearer exchange oversight, and the split of authority between agencies.

Democrats Want to Rewrite the CLARITY Act and Crypto Could Pay the PriceDemocrats are reportedly preparing a major rewrite of the CLARITY Act after their midterm victory.The proposed changes could give the SEC greater oversight of crypto markets. The language, highlighted by… pic.twitter.com/DepyDC7V2J

Democratic majorities are likely to place a crystal-clear emphasis on investor safeguards and enforcement tools before endorsing a broad framework favored by many digital-asset firms.

Quick legislation is not ruled out, but any significant bill that advances could look different and move more slowly than earlier expectations.

Recently, Federal agencies have continued examining registration pathways and rules for crypto trading platforms even as Congress deliberates.

Crypto firms therefore face an evolving patchwork of agency actions while lawmakers work toward a more permanent statutory settlement.

Industry legal observers now see comprehensive market-structure rules crucial for the CLARITY Act potentially slipping into 2027.

Bitcoin’s recent rebound and renewed inflows into spot Bitcoin ETFs show that institutional interest has held up despite the political uncertainty.

Those ETF flows have offered the market some support, yet they do not resolve the regulatory questions still facing exchanges, token issuers, and decentralized-finance projects.

Market participants can already gain exposure through regulated products while much of the underlying industry waits for clearer operating rules.

A longer legislative process would likely preserve that divide, favoring firms able to absorb compliance costs and adapt to agency guidance.

#5164. Poland’s lower house backs sanctions bill covering crypto freezes

The bill is now before the Senate and would broaden the grounds for adding people and companies to Poland’s national sanctions list.

Poland’s lower house passed a bill that would broaden the country’s sanctions framework and explicitly include crypto assets among the funds authorities can freeze when imposing sanctions.

The Sejm approved the government-backed Act on Restrictive Measures on Friday by 240 votes to 202, with one abstention, and forwarded it to the Senate on Monday, according to official parliamentary records. The bill explicitly includes crypto assets, as defined under the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), among financial funds that authorities could freeze when imposing sanctions.

Poland’s interior minister would oversee the national sanctions list, with sanctions-listing decisions taking effect the day after authorities publish a designation. Affected individuals and companies could challenge the decision in administrative court, but the bill allows enforcement before a court ruling.

Poland already maintains a national sanctions list under a 2022 law aimed at countering support for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The bill would expand the grounds for imposing national sanctions to include certain foreign interference and information manipulation that pose a serious threat to national security.

The Senate has 30 days to approve, amend or reject the legislation. If it takes no action, Poland’s Constitution treats the bill as approved in the form passed by the Sejm, allowing it to proceed to the president for consideration.

Looking closer at that list though, and it seemed to be pretty evident that they’re mostly miners.

According to data from Cryptoquant, newer BTC buyers may be hurting too. The short-term holder (STH) SOPR (7d average) had a reading of 0.99 at press time. Anything under 1 essentially means more people are selling at a loss than at a profit.

The RSI was at 33.8, well below the Signal Line and not far from the oversold mark.

So, is a bounce on the way? Well, with fewer loss-making coins on exchanges, sellers are probably running low on steam.

#5162. ARK Invest Trims Block and Bullish Positions as Bitcoin ETF Outflows Continue

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: Disclosed ARK Invest trading activity points to sales of shares in crypto-linked companies Block and Bullish alongside changes elsewhere in its portfolios. A fund manager selling shares is not the same as investors redeeming money from a spot Bitcoin ETF, and the trades should not be treated as a categorical forecast for crypto prices.

Crypto markets generate several types of selling headlines, but they do not all describe the same thing. One involves investors moving money into or out of exchange-traded products. Another involves a fund manager changing which companies it owns inside a portfolio. ARK Invest’s latest trade disclosures belong to the second category.

ARK’s trade-notification service provides information about purchases and sales by its exchange-traded funds. Reporting of the November 9 trades indicates reductions in shares of Block and Bullish, both businesses tied to the wider digital-asset economy.

Trade data published for the session should be checked against the original ARK notification for exact fund allocations and amounts. Public summaries can combine activity across several ETFs, while dollar-value estimates change with the share price used for calculation.

A growth-oriented fund might sell shares to rebalance position weights, manage liquidity, fund purchases of other holdings or respond to company-specific developments. A share sale alone cannot reveal which of those motives dominated.

For that reason, it would be a mistake to describe ARK’s selling as proof that the manager has abandoned Bitcoin. The sale may reflect a view on the risk and valuation of individual equities rather than the future value of the underlying cryptocurrency.

Block’s exposure to digital assets is also different from Bullish’s. Their revenue drivers, regulation and business models are not interchangeable merely because both are routinely grouped under the label ‘crypto stock.’ Investors comparing them need to look beyond the common theme.

NewsBTC has recently tracked sizable outflows from US spot Bitcoin funds and earlier daily Bitcoin ETF withdrawals. Those figures measure net investor flows into or out of specific products, rather than an ETF manager switching between equity holdings.

Even within ETF reporting, transactions can be misunderstood. Selling shares in a listed company held by an actively managed ETF does not necessarily imply the ETF itself suffered a redemption. Likewise, a Bitcoin ETF net outflow does not automatically show why an individual investor chose to redeem.

Those distinctions become especially important in a market where the same financial firm may own Bitcoin directly, operate a fund holding mining or exchange equities, and manage entirely different technology-sector positions.

Shares of trading venues, payment companies and miners are often affected by crypto prices but can also move on earnings results, borrowing costs and capital spending. A mining company pursuing AI infrastructure may be valued on its power contracts as much as its Bitcoin output. A brokerage might add accounts while earning less from crypto transactions.

That mixture means crypto-equity portfolio changes sometimes convey a different message from spot-token trading activity. They are better read as part of ongoing active management than as standalone signals to buy or sell a coin.

The strongest verifiable facts are the securities traded, the direction of the trade and the number of shares reported for each fund. If later reporting establishes exact price-weighted values, those should be dated and described as estimates where appropriate.

ARK’s trading notices offer a window into portfolio decisions, not a complete explanation of motive. Their value for readers comes from knowing precisely what changed and avoiding the temptation to translate every share sale into a broad claim about the Bitcoin market.

#5160. XRP’s Quantum-Resistant Design Comes Into Focus

Home » Ripple (XRP) » XRP’s Quantum-Resistant Design Comes Into Focus

The foundation behind XRP Ledger aims to mitigate quantum resistance hazards ahead of the practical test.

The chain developers behind Ripple’s native XRP Ledger are actively preparing to implement quantum-resistant measures. For this reason, the devs picked ML-DSA-44, a digital signature standard that the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) approved in 2024.

Earlier this year, Ripple introduced a multi-phase roadmap to prepare the XRP Ledger (XRPL) for a post-quantum future, with a target for full readiness by 2028. The new signature format needs 3,732 bytes for public keys and signatures, raising transaction data requirements. This will be audited in mid 2027.

JUST IN: $XRP Ledger unveils quantum-resistant account plan, allowing users to upgrade to quantum-proof security with no additional transaction fees as Ripple targets full quantum protection by 2028. pic.twitter.com/wS2Mk46nG8

As described in Google’s quantum computing research paper, there’s a few key risks the crypto sphere has to handle. The most quoted one is the exposable public key risks when users transact within the blockchain, something that quantum-computing based hackers could take serious advantage of.

There’s a more subtle risk too, one elliptic curve researchers call “harvest now, decrypt later.” Simply put, bad actors can collect publicly visible cryptographic data from the blockchain today and hold onto it. This raises the chances of the account eventually being broken into.

🚨 MASSIVE: THE $XRP LEDGER IS PREPARING FOR QUANTUM COMPUTERS. HERE IS WHAT NOBODY IS TELLING YOU.Every payment you sign reveals your public key.A powerful enough quantum computer could work backward from it.Any account that has ever sent a payment is already exposed.The… https://t.co/hpCLy5Gzzi pic.twitter.com/L32SemqQcE

The extra XRP network storage needed for this kind of upgrade doesn’t necessarily raise the fees. Node operators are absorbing the ~3.6 KB increase per protected transaction (from 105 bytes to 3,732 bytes for key plus the signature), as documented in the proposal. With database overhead, every secure payment would use 5,331 bytes of storage.

David Schwartz Explains What Could Really Drive XRP's ValueFormer Ripple (@Ripple) CTO David Schwartz (@JoelKatz) says using $XRP to pay XRPL (@XRP) gas fees is unlikely to drive its price significantly.He argues that broader network adoption could create value for XRP… pic.twitter.com/X0et9M7El9

The XRP Ledger foundation is planning the inaugural phase of the quantum resistance study in early 2027 as devs polish the proposition of key generation between the Python, JavaScript and server versions. Mitigations are done within a zero-knowledge proof to validate results without disclosing vectors.

Quantum physics may be a tough nut to crack for most crypto currencies, but XRP’s developers are set on a mission to get the chain shielded by 2028.

Compare fees, cashback, availability, and features of 12 crypto cards to find the right option for your spending needs.

Crypto debit cards are no longer just a way to convert Bitcoin into cash for everyday purchases. In 2026, there are plenty of options, from exchange-linked cards and stablecoin payment solutions to self-custody cards connected directly to crypto wallets.

But choosing one isn’t just about cashback. Availability depends on your country, better rewards may require staking or a paid subscription, and fees can quickly eat into your benefits. It’s also worth checking how each card works, as some are prepaid debit cards while others offer credit backed by crypto holdings.

We’ve selected 12 crypto cards worth considering in 2026, comparing their features, fees, rewards, and availability to help you find the right option, whether you prioritize low fees, stablecoin spending, cashback, or control over your assets.

The Coinbase Card Visa prepaid debit card that lets US customers (excluding Hawaii) spend directly from their Coinbase accounts.

It is a custodial card, meaning funds remain in your Coinbase account and are deducted when you make a purchase. Coinbase automatically converts crypto to USD at checkout or for ATM withdrawals, so merchants never receive crypto. You also get a virtual card as soon as you’re approved, with Apple Pay and Google Pay support.

Fees are relatively low. There are no annual fees or charges for spending USD or crypto, including USDC. Coinbase Card does not charge monthly or foreign transaction fees, and there are no Coinbase ATM withdrawal fees (though ATM operators may charge their own). The main cost is Coinbase’s crypto conversion spread. Spending USD or USDC avoids it, making them the cheapest funding options.

Crypto rewards are the main attraction, but rates vary. Rewards are optional, available to US users, and paid in a crypto asset of your choice from a rotating list. Rates are displayed in the app, can be changed at any time, and have no stated cap. Although many reviews advertise rates of up to 4%, Coinbase does not guarantee a fixed rate on its official card page. Check the current in-app offer before applying.

Best for: US-based Coinbase users who want a simple, low-fee card and crypto rewards without a credit check.

Crypto.com’s crypto debit card depends on your region. In the US, it is now a Visa Signature credit card issued by Comenity Capital Bank through Bread Financial. Cardholders can earn rewards in BTC or CRO, but approval requires a credit check. Applications are made through the Crypto.com app.

Rewards range from roughly 1.5% to 5–6%, depending on the tier. However, higher Level Up tiers require locking up or staking CRO. Those who don’t want to commit CRO can choose the entry tier.

Outside the US, the card remains a prepaid debit card. In the European Economic Area (EEA), the free tier offers no cashback, while the Plus plan (€4.99/month) starts at 2% cashback.

Best for: Users who already hold CRO and want to maximize rewards.

KAST is a Visa debit card that that spends a USD balance funded with stablecoins. It offers three tiers: Standard (free, 1.5% cashback), Premium ($1000 a year, 2% cashback) and Private ($10,000 a year, 3%).

Cashback is paid in dollars, rather than tokens. Monthly cashback limits apply: $2,000 in spend for Standard, $10,000 for Premium and $40,000 for Private.

However, KAST fees can reduce the returns. Foreign exchange fees on KAS crypto debit card range from 0.5% to 1.75%, while a physical Standard card costs $40 to deliver.

KAST estimates Standard users may keep up to 1% cashback after FX fees. Premium and Private also include a Visa Infinite card and KAST Points on eligible spending.

Best for: Fequent stablecoin spenders, especially those spending in USD.

Krak, Kraken’s money app, launched its Visa debit card in the US in August 2026. Available as a physical and virtual card, it lets users spend from 600+ fiat and crypto assets, with purchases converted to USD at checkout. The card is issued by Lead Bank and powered by Stripe Issuing.

Krak offers up to 2% cashback in USD or Bitcoin, paid after transactions settle, with no monthly or annual fees.

Rewards depend on users’ average asset balances across Krak, Kraken and Kraken Pro. The card is available in all US states except New York, Maine, Massachusetts and Indiana. Crypto-funded purchases may incur conversion spreads and trigger taxable events.

Best for: US users who hold a mix of crypto and cash and want one card for everything.

The MetaMask Card lets users spend directly from their self-custody wallet, without preloading funds. Built with Mastercard and Baanx (now Monavate) and issued by Cross River Bank in the US, it works wherever Mastercard is accepted, including online, in-store and through Apple Pay or Google Pay. Unlike exchange cards, MetaMask Card allows to retain full control of your crypto until purchase.

The card has two tiers: the standard card offers 1% cashback in mUSD, while the Metal card costs $199/year and offers 3% cashback on up to $10,000 in annual spending, no foreign transaction fees and higher limits.

Outside the US, it is available in Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Colombia, the EEA, Mexico, Switzerland and the UK. The trade-off is that users take full responsibility for securing their own assets.

Best for: Existing MetaMask users who want to keep control of their keys.

The Nexo Card is a Mastercard issued by DiPocket UAB, a Lithuanian-licensed e-money institution (EMI). It offers two app-controlled modes: Credit Mode, which lets users borrow against their crypto without selling it, and Debit Mode.

Cashback depends on Nexo’s loyalty tier, portfolio balance, and card mode. Rewards are paid in NEXO tokens or BTC, with payouts changeable at any time. Rates can reach 2% in NEXO or 0.5% in BTC, although Nexo’s regional page lists up to 2% cashback for credit card holders.

The card is available to eligible users in selected European markets, including the EEA and UK.

Best for: European long-term holders who want liquidity without selling.

The Bybit Card is a Mastercard debit card linked to your Bybit account. In the EEA and Switzerland, it is issued by Moorwand Ltd and Harmoniie SAS, with a 0.5% FX fee on top of Mastercard’s rate and a 0.9% crypto conversion fee.

Availability is limited to selected markets, including the EEA, Switzerland, Australia, Argentina, Brazil, parts of Asia Pacific, and Mexico.

Rewards depend on spending tiers or VIP status, not a flat cashback rate. The advertised “up to 10%” applies only to top tiers.

Fees and limits vary by region, and cashback without VIP status can be minimal, particularly outside Europe. US users should consider alternatives.

Best for: Non-US Bybit traders who want to spend without leaving the crypto exchange.

RedotPay is a custodial Visa card for global stablecoin users, allowing crypto spending in over 100 countries.

It costs $10 for a virtual card or $100 for a physical one, with no monthly or annual fees, and supports major assets including USDT, USDC, BTC, ETH, BNB and SOL.

Standard pricing includes a 1% crypto-to-fiat conversion fee for USD transactions and an additional 1.2% FX markup.

Standard RedotPay accounts offer no ongoing cashback, relying on welcome bonuses and referral rewards. However, its optional RedotPay Pro membership offers 3% cashback on eligible Apple Pay and Google Pay purchases.

The card is unavailable in the US, Canada, China, Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Russia.

Best for: Freelancers and remote workers paid in USDT outside the US.

Uphold relaunched its US debit card in October 2025, advertising up to 6% in XRP rewards, with additional benefits for direct deposit users. Actual rates vary by tier and conditions, with some sources citing up to 4%. The US offers Essential and Elite plans, both paying rewards exclusively in XRP.

Essential has no annual fee but charges $4.99 for a physical card, $2.95 per ATM withdrawal, and $1.50 in foreign transaction fees.

Elite costs $99.99 annually, includes a metal card, and waives Uphold ATM and foreign transaction fees.

Crypto-funded spending may involve spreads and taxable events. Availability varies by state, while UK users receive a separate program offering 1% cashback in GBP.

Best for: US users who want a multi-asset card and are comfortable earning XRP.

Ether.fi Cash is a non-custodial Visa card that connects DeFi assets to everyday spending. Users can pay directly with USDC or LiquidUSD, or borrow against their crypto without selling it.

The card combines debit-style direct payments with crypto-backed credit. Rewards reach 3% in USDC for most users and 4% for VIP members on the first $50,000.

It offers up to 3% cashback in USDC for most users, rising to 4% for VIP members on the first $50,000 spent. Fees and eligibility vary by tier and region, with some benefits requiring ETHFI staking.

Best for: experienced DeFi users already inside the ether.fi ecosystem.

The Bitpanda Card is a simple Visa debit card for EEA residents. It is available in all Eurozone countries except Cyprus, and requires a verified Bitpanda account and the mobile app.

The card offers 1% cashback on eligible crypto spending, access to more than 600 crypto assets, no monthly fee and no FX fees charged by Bitpanda, although Visa mark-ups may apply.

There are a few important exclusions: stablecoins, precious metals, Bitpanda Stocks and fiat balances do not qualify for cashback. Each payment also triggers a trade, meaning standard trading fees apply. ATM withdrawals cost 2%, with a minimum fee of €2.

Best for: Euro-area users who already invest with Bitpanda.

Gate Card is a custodial crypto debit card linked to your Gate account, available in virtual and physical Visa or Mastercard versions, depending on region. Compatible cards support Apple Pay and Google Pay, with instant virtual issuance.

Cashback ranges from 1% to 8%, depending on your VIP tier or monthly spending. Rewards are issued as points redeemable for USDT, GT and other supported assets, subject to monthly limits of $5–$400.

Fees vary by card, but the latest Blue and AI versions offer free issuance and no monthly fee, with a 0.9% top-up fee and 1.5–1.7% FX fee. Their limits reach $150,000 daily and $1 million monthly.

Level 2 KYC is required. The international service excludes certain jurisdictions, including the US, where a separate Gate US Visa card is available under different terms.

Best for: Existing Gate users who want crypto spending with tier-based rewards and are comfortable keeping funds on a custodial exchange.

The best crypto debit card depends on how you plan to use it, where you live, and which features matter most. Before applying, consider these five factors:

Not every crypto card works worldwide. Some are restricted to the US, EEA, UK, or selected countries. Check whether the provider supports residents of your country and whether the card offers the same features in your region.

Look beyond monthly and annual fees. Crypto conversion spreads, foreign exchange markups, ATM withdrawal charges, and card issuance costs can all affect how much you actually spend.

Compare the rewards you can realistically earn, not just the highest advertised percentage. Some providers require staking, paid subscriptions, or minimum spending levels to unlock better rates. Also check whether rewards are paid in cash, stablecoins, or volatile crypto assets.

Exchange-linked cards generally rely on custodial accounts, while self-custody products can allow users to retain control of their assets until payment. Understand who controls your funds and what happens if your account or wallet is compromised.

Some crypto cards offer prepaid spending, while others provide credit backed by crypto collateral. These products have different risks, repayment requirements, and potential tax implications. Make sure you understand which type you are applying for.

Traditional debit cards use money held in a bank account, while crypto debit cards are linked to cryptocurrency exchanges, digital wallets or stablecoin balances.

When making a payment, some crypto cards automatically convert your digital assets into fiat currency. Others let you spend stablecoins directly or borrow against your crypto holdings.

The main differences come down to funding, custody, fees and rewards. Crypto cards can offer cashback in digital assets and easier access to crypto funds, but may also involve conversion fees, additional account requirements and tax implications.

In some jurisdictions, spending crypto is treated as a taxable disposal. It’s worth checking the local tax rules before using crypto for everyday payments.

Crypto debit cards make it easier to use digital assets for everyday purchases, whether through crypto-funded payments, stablecoin spending or cashback rewards.

But the benefits aren’t always as good as they look. Conversion spreads, foreign transaction fees, subscription costs and staking requirements can eat into your rewards.

The best card depends on how you plan to use it. If low fees matter most, an exchange-linked card may be enough. If you prefer greater control over your assets or want to spend stablecoins, other options may be more suitable. For cashback, look beyond the advertised rate and factor in all associated costs.

Ultimately, choose a card that fits your spending habits, location and risk tolerance. Check the latest fees and terms, and don’t overlook potential tax implications.

A crypto debit card is a payment card linked to a cryptocurrency exchange account or digital wallet. It allows users to make purchases at merchants that accept its payment network, with crypto or stablecoins converted into fiat currency when required.

No. Availability depends on the card issuer, payment provider, and local regulations. Some cards are restricted to US residents, while others support selected European, Asian, or Latin American markets. Features and fees may also differ between regions.

Some crypto debit cards have no annual or monthly fees, but other costs may apply. These include crypto conversion spreads, foreign exchange fees, ATM withdrawal charges, issuance fees, and paid membership subscriptions.

It depends on the card. Many custodial cards convert cryptocurrency into fiat currency when a payment is processed. Some self-custody cards allow users to retain control of their assets until the transaction takes place, while crypto-backed credit products may allow spending without an immediate sale.

Tax treatment depends on your country and the type of reward. Spending appreciated cryptocurrency may trigger a taxable disposal, while cashback and promotional rewards can have different tax treatment. Consult the applicable tax rules in your jurisdiction.

#5155. This Bitcoin Developer’s Idea Would Make Quantum Attacks a Losing Bet

This Bitcoin Developer’s Idea Would Make Quantum Attacks a Losing Bet

Bitcoin developer Cory Fields has an unusual idea for dealing with future quantum thieves: Make them risk their own Bitcoin every time they try to steal someone else’s.

In a November 4 post to the Bitcoin development mailing list, Fields outlined “quantum landmines” and two types of auctions designed to turn attacks on vulnerable wallets into expensive gambles. He called the ideas “thought experiments,” not a completed Bitcoin upgrade.

Bitcoin owners use a secret private key to authorize transactions. A matching public key lets the network check their signatures without learning the secret.

If the whole idea seems too hard to understand, we used AI to generate a video to help you grasp it:

Today’s computers cannot realistically calculate that private key from the public one. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could use a mathematical technique called Shor’s algorithm to do it, potentially letting a thief spend coins as if they owned them.

Some older Bitcoin outputs have exposed public keys, and certain newer formats reveal them too. Other addresses hide the key until someone spends, so the risk is not identical for every wallet.

Researchers call the hypothetical arrival of a computer capable of these attacks “Q-Day.” No publicly demonstrated machine can steal Bitcoin this way today, and nobody knows exactly when one might exist.

Imagine someone owns 1 BTC in an old, potentially vulnerable wallet. Before Q-Day, this person creates a tiny, separate quantum-safe Bitcoin output containing a hidden proof that they controlled the original private key while quantum theft was still impossible.

Think of it as a sealed ownership receipt. Outsiders can see the small output, but not the evidence tucked inside it, or even that it is a trap.

Now imagine a future thief uses a quantum computer to recover the user’s old private key. Under Fields’s suggested rules, the thief cannot simply take her 1 BTC: They must add 1 BTC of their own from a quantum-safe wallet as collateral.

Both coins enter a restricted output worth 2 BTC. The thief must wait through a challenge period—30 days in Fields’s example—before spending it freely.

The wallet owner notices the transaction and reveals the pre-Q-Day proof. The network then allows the owner to move the full 2 BTC to the quantum-safe address they committed to earlier: their original coin, plus the thief’s collateral.

The attacker has no way to know in advance which old wallets contain these hidden receipts. Even a successful quantum key recovery could become a 1 BTC loss.

The wallet owner would also need matching collateral to initiate a normal post-Q-Day move of her own legacy coin. If they have no spare BTC, the same rule intended to hurt thieves could make moving her savings difficult.

Landmines only work when an owner prepares one before Q-Day and reveals it in time. They cannot protect coins whose keys are already lost, including some of the early Bitcoin holdings widely believed to be inaccessible.

Fields proposes a second mechanism called a staked auction. Before Q-Day, someone could lock up quantum-safe Bitcoin and secretly register a bid against a specific old wallet they expect thieves to target.

Suppose an apparently abandoned wallet holds 50 BTC. A future attacker tries to move it and posts another 50 BTC as collateral; during the auction period, someone who committed a bid in advance can challenge the attempted theft.

In Fields’s example, a successful challenger claims part of the attacker’s collateral while the original vulnerable coins are destroyed rather than awarded to the bidder. The point is to deprive thieves of a reliable payday, not return the coins to a missing owner.

His third idea, a sats auction, requires no advance stake. Instead, a vulnerable-coin spend would trigger a contest in which the highest bidder gets the coins minus their bid, while the runner-up pays their bid and gets nothing.

That resembles a notorious auction game where two bidders keep raising their offers because neither wants to be the person who loses money for nothing. A thief might avoid starting a contest that could cost more than the coins they hoped to steal.

One proposed response to quantum risk is to restrict spending from outdated wallets after a migration deadline. That might prevent theft, but could also permanently lock out legitimate owners who never moved their coins.

Fields is exploring a different trade-off: Keep old coins potentially spendable, but make attempted transfers costly and open to challenges. Bitcoin cannot tell an honest owner from a quantum thief if both can produce the same valid signature.

The trade-off is severe, considering that honest owners might need large collateral deposits, inactive holders could miss their chance to object, and auction rules might burn coins belonging to people who are still alive and simply offline.

Bitcoin would first need a quantum-safe way to hold and spend funds. Wallets would then need to support hidden ownership commitments, while Bitcoin’s consensus rules would have to enforce collateral, waiting periods, special recovery transactions, and auctions.

Developers would also need to agree on when the new rules activate, how much collateral is required, and what happens to losing bids or leftover funds. Fields believes some mechanics could be introduced through a soft fork, a type of Bitcoin rule change, but has not supplied the detailed design.

None of these protections exists in Bitcoin today. Fields has published no implementation or activation schedule, and his original post leaves the auction payouts and even the desired outcome of an auction unresolved.

#5154. October CPI sparks another crypto wipeout, but is buying the Bitcoin dip too risky?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Is the post-CPI FUD creating another opportunity to buy the fear?

Santiment analysts seem to think so. According to their report, retailers are becoming extremely bearish with only 0.82 bullish comments for every bearish comment on Bitcoin. However, this level of pessimism could signal a contrarian buying opportunity, as extreme retail fear has historically been seen near market bottoms.

The timing is no coincidence. Retail optimism has been fading as the U.S economy continues to deal with sticky inflation. U.S headline CPI was up 0.4% in October compared to expectations of 0.3% and core CPI increased by 0.3% versus expectations of 0.2%. The result? A shift in market expectations.

As can be seen in the chart above, expectations for rate hikes have been rising quickly. For instance, the chances of a 50 basis point increase in December have risen to 11%, while there is an expectation of a 25 basis point increase of 84%. This puts the Fed’s December decision back in focus.

And, the concerns do not stop there. Peter Schiff has also commented on the concern around sustained inflation. He noted how the CPI increased by 0.4% in October, taking the total increase in 2026 to 4.15%, with two months still left in the year. If the trend continues, the inflation could increase to 5% by the end of the year, adding further pressure on the Fed to keep monetary policy tight.

This means that Bitcoin [BTC] may be recording a hike in retail pessimism, with the same coinciding with increasingly bearish macro outlooks. This can be seen as a positive for Santiment’s contrarian indicator, but will the heightened macro risk mean that it is too risky to “buy the dip?”

The post-CPI reaction has triggered another crypto wipeout too.

Interestingly, there have been three instances of long liquidations above $500 million in under two weeks since November started. This alludes to huge waves of deleveraging in the market as traders get squeezed out of their longs. And yet, despite these leverage resets, there still seemed to be a prevalent bearish bias.

More importantly, on-chain data has been adding to the pressure. The supply of Tether has been shrinking at a much faster rate than when FTX collapsed.

Over the last 60 days, for instance, USDT’s market cap fell by $6.6 billion, more than double the amount it fell during December 2022. Meanwhile, as Bitcoin fell from $79,000 to $73,000 last week, large holders reduced their balances by more than 34,000 BTC, worth roughly $2.6 billion.

In essence, the market is not showing clear signs of contrarian buying just yet.

Instead, reduced liquidity and a lack of solid smart money accumulation suggested that this downtrend may not be indicative of the usual short-term to long-term holder transition phase. This would make retail pessimism a weaker bottom signal, especially as large holders continue to reduce their exposure.

Consequently, this puts Santiment’s contrarian indicator in question. Considering inflation worries, increasing December rate hike expectations, and weak on-chain indicators, the risk to reward on this Bitcoin dip could be unfavorable. Especially since the market could still be facing a deeper correction.

Rising retail fear could create a Bitcoin buying opportunity, but inflation and rate-hike concerns are adding pressure.

Falling liquidity, whale selling, and heavy long liquidations mean the market could face further downside.

#5153. Bitcoin nears 11-week low after ‘discouraging’ US CPI inflation beat

Bitcoin and US stocks initially fall after October inflation tops forecasts, with traders expecting a quarter-point Fed rate hike in December.

Bitcoin (BTC) dipped toward its 11-week lows near $73,500 at Tuesday’s Wall Street open after US inflation came above expectations.

Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD falling to $73,518, nearly matching the low it set on Sunday, its lowest level since Aug. 21.

BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

The October print of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) came in at 0.4% month-on-month, above the anticipated 0.3%. CPI, which lacked a year-on-year component due to the absence of data collection during the 2025 US government shutdown, nonetheless showed a cooling rate of growth versus September, when the monthly increase hit 0.6%.

“The index for shelter rose 0.3 percent in October, accounting for over thirty percent of the monthly all items increase. The food index increased 0.5 percent in October, as the food at home index rose 0.4 percent and the food away from home index increased 0.5 percent,” the official release from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) stated.

Whereas energy price increases had accounted for a major portion of the September CPI gain, October’s energy index advanced significantly less at 0.7% versus the previous 5.2% move.

Economist Robin Brooks described the CPI result as “discouraging” while noting that the oil-price spike had contributed to the September numbers.

“All the details of this CPI report are discouraging, but October was also the peak of the second big oil price shock this year and that’s obviously going to bleed into core CPI inflation,” he wrote in an analysis.

In a speech earlier on Tuesday, Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller said that he favored hiking interest rates by 25 basis points in December even if inflation cooled from September. Data from CME Group’s FedWatch Tool showed markets pricing in a 96.3% chance of that outcome at the Fed’s December meeting as a result.

Following the CPI report, those odds turned more hawkish, with a 25-basis-point hike attracting 85.3% odds and a 50-basis-point hike attracting 14.7%.

Fed target-rate probability comparison for December FOMC meeting (screenshot). Source: CME Group

Related: Here’s what happened in crypto today

US stocks came under pressure at the Wall Street open as CPI added to existing headwinds for bulls. These included strong labor-market data and the prospect of tighter AI-sector regulation under a Democratic-controlled House and Senate.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index opened down 0.6% before recouping the losses, while Nvidia stock fell nearly 4% amid a board investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

Nvidia stock one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

“Consumer inflation has continued running above target while the October jobs report removed any concerns about a slowdown in the labor market,” trading resource Mosaic Asset Company summarized in analysis on the day.

Mosaic nonetheless observed signs of “extreme” sell-side pressure on the Nasdaq, potentially signaling that the index had formed a long-term bottom.

“That includes a spike in the equity put/call ratio which jumped over 1.0 and is even higher than during the trade war selloff in April 2025,” it added.

Nasdaq Composite Index one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

#5152. End of Crypto Hardware Wallets? Sui Cancels Suiball Wallet Amid Cybersecurity Risks

The hardware wallets industry is taking a huge hit in 2026, and Ledger's supply chain exploit set a certain fact in stone: no wallet is secure, no algorithm is uncrackable. As a reminder: back in October, Ledger confirmed the placement of an unauthorized electronic plate inside of their device sold via reseller CryptoBills.

Units sold in Southeast Asia had an exploit which allowed illicit actors to steal recovery phrases during the setup of the wallet.

Most likely outcome for the cybersecurity industry would be AI protecting itself from AI-based reverse-engineering. This is not taking into consideration things like one happened with Ledger.

Sui Hardware wallet is no different: they understand the risks and take them seriously on such extent where they simply decide not to ship it, avoiding unnecessary risks. Suiball, a hardware wallet built natively for Sui, announced its closure on November 11, after the Sui Foundation decided that backing a hardware wallet project is too risky after the recent attacks across the industry.

Surprisingly, the first batch of wallets have already been developed, manufactured and ready to be sent out to the first owners. However, the Sui Foundation decided to play it safe and avoid potential issues with those who might want to reverse-engineer the wallet or plant a backdoor somewhere along the supply chain.

The recent Fable 5.2 release suggests an advanced level of work with electronics, hardware devices and firmwares, which is the exact field hackers might need to attack hardware wallets using AI. Anthropic states that Fable 5.2, released on November 9, designed three working devices from one-paragraph prompts.

Those devices went through the whole cycle with its partner Diode, including schematics, circuit boards and firmware. Luckily, there's no proven link between the Fable 5.2 release and Suiball's closure, as the project hasn't mentioned AI at all.

Most of the hardware wallets pre-orders were on-chain, so users will simply receive their USDC back.

Around 80% of all orders were placed this way, and refunds will reach the wallets holding the soulbound pre-order NFTs within a week. Users do not need to take any action.

Users who purchased their wallets with credit or debit cards will also receive their funds back. But in order to get refunded successfully, Sui urges buyers to contact them by email first. After the refund is completed, all personal data of purchasers will be deleted.

#5150. Nvidia Board Investigates Jensen Huang After Report He Was Target of Chinese Spy Effort

Nvidia Board Investigates Jensen Huang After Report He Was Target of Chinese Spy Effort

Nvidia's board of directors has opened an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the company said on Sunday.

A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, will oversee the inquiry. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," it said, adding that it "has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team."

We just issued a press release from our board of directors. Read the release: https://t.co/W9yXWJzbkk

— NVIDIA Newsroom (@nvidianewsroom) November 8, 2026

The investigation follows a Financial Times report on Saturday that a U.S. government memo, written earlier this year based on intelligence information, said the Nvidia CEO had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, citing people familiar with the memo. U.S. intelligence believes she was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, the FT reported. Nvidia declined to comment to the newspaper on the memo. Huang's email to staff, sent on Sunday, did not name the person with whom he had an affair.

Lawmakers from both parties are seeking answers. Republican leaders have asked Huang to appear privately before the House China, foreign affairs and intelligence committees, according to the FT, while Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE), who will chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee from January, pledged in a tweet that "Congress will investigate and get answers."

The FT's report built on a New York Times investigation last month, which said U.S. intelligence agencies had concluded that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, was a Chinese intelligence asset, and that surveillance of her had revealed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. President Donald Trump was briefed on the findings roughly a year ago and chose not to act on them, according to the Times.

U.S. officials suspected Megaspeed of helping Chinese companies get around restrictions on advanced AI chips, and the Commerce Department's investigation into the company has been handed to the Justice Department, the Times reported. Megaspeed's sister company in Malaysia bought at least $4.8 billion worth of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records cited by the newspaper.

Nvidia told the Times that Huang's interactions with Ms. Huang were "not unusual or unexpected," and that customers like Megaspeed receive "ordinary business information." Megaspeed said it had retained outside counsel to conduct an internal investigation, Ms. Huang did not respond to the newspaper's requests for comment, and China's embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations as "groundless smears and slanders."

In an email to employees on Sunday, Huang apologized to his family and colleagues. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," he wrote, according to a copy published by CNBC.

"Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," the company told CNBC.

Nvidia shares were down 5% at $177.32 in premarket trading early on Monday, after closing at $186.64 on Friday, according to Yahoo Finance.

#5149. Deutsche Bank Opens Digital Asset Custody to Paying Institutional Clients

Deutsche Bank opens up digital asset custody to paying institutional clients. The service includes storage, user experience improvements, and accessibility via the bank's own gateways. The bank announced the launch on November 11, as DB's official website reveals.

This is an improvement in the field of institutional adoption, even though it comes at a time when it might be unwarranted. The market is experiencing serious issues and constant outflows from both retail and institutional investors.

Surprisingly, the bank can provide both warm and cold storage options available directly through DB's infrastructure. According to the landing page, the platform will provide key storage via Hardware Security Modules. Access goes through Autobahn, the bank's own multi-channel gateway.

Compliance will also be handled by Deutsche Bank. Initially, the service will focus on core functions: custody of digital assets and transfers, with further capabilities planned.

The Asian market has yet to receive similar treatment. For now, the service is available in the EU, operating out of DB AG Frankfurt. An expansion to Asia is reportedly planned for 2027, though the details are yet to be confirmed.

Additionally, DB announced support for euro stablecoins such as EURC and EURAU, in addition to BTC, ETH, and USDC. This is an attempt to promote the adoption of EU-issued stablecoins as part of a strategy aimed at moving away from USDT dominance. EURAU is issued by AllUnity, a joint venture that includes DWS, the asset manager majority-owned by Deutsche Bank.

Self-custody or banks: that is the real question here. Industry experts such as Bloomberg's ETF analyst Eric Balchunas suggest that self-custody has been a worse option and that a custodian with funds protection and insurance is a better option for regular investors. Even Binance founder CZ admitted after the Ledger incident that self-custody comes with extra responsibilities.

Back in August, a Coldcard exploit drained 1,816 BTC from more than 5,000 cold-storage addresses, according to Fortune.

However, it puts some pressure on those who might receive their funds from grey sources. Unfortunately for them, a bank custodian creates another barrier, as every deposit has to go through the bank's compliance checks.

#5148. Why Is Bitcoin Down Today? Key Factors Behind BTC’s Slide Toward $73K

Home » Bitcoin (BTC) » Why Is Bitcoin Down Today? Key Factors Behind BTC’s Slide Toward $73K

Bitcoin’s decline comes as market sentiment weakens, raising questions about whether the latest pullback could deepen.

Bitcoin fell to $73,770 on November 11, with several warning signals emerging across financial markets as pressure on the cryptocurrency mounted.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency dropped 1.6% over the past 24 hours. BTC briefly fell to $72,740 on November 10 before recovering some ground.

Meanwhile, the broader crypto market is showing signs of growing anxiety. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index has fallen to 35, placing sentiment firmly in the Fear zone. This marks a further deterioration from last week’s and last month’s reading of 46, which indicated Neutral sentiment.

So, what is driving Bitcoin lower? Four developments are putting pressure on the cryptocurrency, with unexpectedly high US inflation emerging as the biggest concern.

The biggest pressure on Bitcoin price comes from the latest US inflation figures.

October’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.4%, exceeding economists’ expectations of 0.3%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy prices, also came in hotter than expected, rising 0.3% against forecasts of 0.2%.

The figures have raised concerns that the Federal Reserve could increase interest rates in December rather than ease monetary policy.

According to CME Group’s FedWatch tool, interest rate futures now imply an 88.5% probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike next month.

That shift matters for Bitcoin because higher interest rates generally make riskier assets less attractive. When borrowing costs rise and safer investments offer better returns, investors may reduce exposure to speculative assets such as cryptocurrencies.

Another source of weakness is the persistent withdrawal of money from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

These funds have recorded approximately $2.15 billion in net outflows since October 30, according to SoSoValue data.

The situation became particularly concerning last Friday, when US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $696 million in single-day outflows, their largest daily withdrawal since January, according to Glassnode.

“Only two days in the past year saw larger outflows, and both came before price fell further,” Glassnode noted in a post on X.

ETF investors are selling bitcoin:native again.US spot ETFs saw $696M of net outflows on Friday, the largest single day since January.Only two days in the past year saw larger outflows, and both came before price fell further. A return to steady inflows would ease that… pic.twitter.com/q9mnj4FWFf

The analytics firm added that a return to consistent inflows would help ease the selling pressure.

The sell-off has also been amplified by forced liquidations in the crypto derivatives market.

More than $742 million worth of crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, according to CoinGlass data. Around $583 million came from long positions, meaning traders who had bet on rising prices.

Broader financial markets are also becoming less supportive of Bitcoin.

The US Dollar Index, which tracks the dollar against six major currencies, rose 0.1% to 102.30, nearing its highest level since October 29. Meanwhile, the yield on the US 10-year Treasury note moved closer to 5%.

Experts agree that both trends can weigh on Bitcoin. A stronger dollar and higher bond yields make traditional investments more attractive, giving investors less reason to take risks on assets like cryptocurrencies.

Derivatives analytics platform CoinGlass recently flagged $74,400 as a key level for BTC, warning that a sustained breakdown beneath it would confirm a bearish bias.

Additionally, Bitcoin recently closed its fifth consecutive red weekly candle while slipping below its 50-week moving average at the similar levels.

Analysts warned that failing to quickly reclaim this key moving average makes a drop toward $70,000 highly probable for Bitcoin.

#5145. Trump Says He Knows 'Nothing' About World Liberty Financial as He Defends UAE Ties

Trump Says He Knows 'Nothing' About World Liberty Financial as He Defends UAE Ties

U.S. President Donald Trump has defended his family's stake in crypto venture World Liberty Financial, saying he knows "nothing" about the firm despite being a co-owner, in an interview after last week's midterm elections.

Asked by columnist Ross Douthat why his co-ownership of a company partly owned by investors linked to the United Arab Emirates government was different from the kind of arrangement he would call corrupt if it involved the Biden family, Trump replied: "Here's the difference [... ] I'm gonna tell you why. Because I know nothing about it," according to a transcript published by CBS News.

Pressed on why he did not simply divest, Trump said most of his money is managed by Wall Street firms through index funds, and that his sons run the family business. "It's hard to say to them, 'Don't do anything anymore for four years because I'm president,'" he said.

When Douthat asked whether foreign investors in the company believe they are buying influence, Trump said: "I don't know." He argued that conflicts of interest have dogged presidents "going back to George Washington," adding that past presidents "own something, whatever crypto was at the time."

"There's crypto, and before that there was oil," Trump said, adding that, "every president has had this problem."

"I'm a bigger name than other presidents, whether we like it or not," Trump said.

World Liberty Financial, which Eric Trump announced in August 2024, issues the WLFI governance token and the USD1 stablecoin. In January, it launched World Liberty Markets, a lending and borrowing platform built on DeFi protocol Dolomite.

Its UAE links have drawn scrutiny from Democrats. Aryam Investment, a UAE-backed entity tied to the country's national security adviser, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed, agreed to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty Financial for $500 million four days before Trump's January 2025 inauguration, Decrypt reported in February, citing The Wall Street Journal. The deal, signed by Eric Trump on World Liberty's behalf, reportedly preceded the administration's reversal of restrictions on advanced AI chip sales to the UAE. A World Liberty spokesperson said at the time that neither Trump nor his Middle East envoy, Steve Witkoff, had "any involvement whatsoever" in the transaction, ABC News reported. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-CT) described the arrangement in February as "potentially criminal conduct." Trump has previously said he was not aware of the deal.

The company's UAE ties have also surfaced in its legal battle with Tron founder Justin Sun. Sun's lawyers asked a federal court to sanction World Liberty, alleging the firm delayed disclosing UAE ownership that could defeat federal jurisdiction over his lawsuit. World Liberty has called Sun's legal campaign a "meritless PR stunt."

The Trump family's financial stake in the venture is set out in World Liberty's own disclosures. DT Marks DEFI LLC, an entity affiliated with Trump and certain family members, owns about 38% of the holding company behind World Liberty Financial, holds 22.5 billion WLFI tokens, and is entitled to 75% of the net proceeds from WLFI token sales, according to the company. A separate Trump-affiliated entity has an indirect claim on interest earned on the reserves backing USD1. The disclosures state that no member of the Trump family is an officer, director or employee of World Liberty, though Trump's sons have remained involved with the company, Decrypt reported earlier this year.

#5144. Does Holding Crypto Put Your Social Security at Risk in 2026?

Home » Cryptopedia » Does Holding Crypto Put Your Social Security at Risk in 2026?

Understanding SSA rules on digital assets and how ABLE accounts can legally protect your benefits.

Short answer: It depends on the type of Social Security benefits you receive.

If you receive Social Security Retirement or SSDI benefits, owning Bitcoin or other crypto generally won’t affect your monthly Social Security payments, as both of these programs don’t have asset limits.

However, if you receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI), things are different. The Social Security Administration (SSA) counts crypto as a resource. If your total countable assets exceed $2,000 for an individual, your SSI benefits could be reduced or suspended.

Note: The figures above are taken from the SSA 2026 COLA fact sheet and the SSA’s ABLE spotlight.

Much of the online confusion around cryptocurrency and Social Security stems from mixing up earned benefits with means-tested benefits:

The Social Security Administration’s (SSA) official Program Operations Manual System (POMS SI 01140.208 and SI 00830.102) outlines explicit rules for digital assets:

Consider an SSI recipient who holds $1,500 in a traditional bank account and receives $600 worth of Bitcoin as a gift:

Crypto’s market volatility introduces a unique risk for benefit compliance. If your wallet balance sits at $1,800 on October 25th, but a market surge pushes its dollar value to $2,200 on November 1st, you are technically over the SSI resource limit for November.

SSA requires beneficiaries to report changes in resources by the 10th day of the month following the change. Thus, logically, recipients must maintain accurate exchange statements, wallet screenshots, and transaction logs to verify historical values.

If you receive SSI and wish to save money without breaching resource caps, an Achieving a Better Life Experience (ABLE) account provides a legal shield:

Note: Check whether your state’s specific ABLE plan offers crypto-indexed investment options before transferring digital assets into the program.

Yes. Under the Access to Financial Institutions (AFI) program and POMS SI 01140.208 reporting procedures, SSA verifies asset balances. Recipients are legally required to disclose digital exchange accounts and self-custody wallet addresses. Failing to report crypto can lead to overpayment penalties or fraud investigations.

Cashing out converts one countable resource (crypto) into another (cash). The total dollar amount still applies to your $2,000 resource limit. However, if you sell at a profit, any capital gains can be counted as unearned income in the month realized, which could reduce or eliminate that month’s SSI check before the cash is evaluated as a resource the following month.

No. Transferring or gifting assets for less than fair market value to satisfy the $2,000 limit triggers a transfer penalty. SSA can impose a period of ineligibility for up to 36 months depending on the value of the crypto given away.

Not directly as coins. ABLE accounts only accept contributions in U.S. dollars. To move crypto into an ABLE account, you must first liquidate the cryptocurrency into cash and deposit the cash into the ABLE account (up to the $20,000 annual limit for 2026). Once inside, the funds are shielded up to $100,000 from the SSI resource test.

#5142. Polymarket US trading volume jumps 266% despite regulatory battles

Trading volume on Polymarket’s US exchange surged from June to October, fueled by sports betting, even as the platform faces mounting regulatory scrutiny.

Trading on Polymarket’s US exchange more than tripled between June and October, up about 266% as the company faced state and federal scrutiny.

Monthly volume rose to $14.77 billion from $4.04 billion over that period, according to data from analytics platform TickerTracker, which counts trades at the contracts’ full payout value.

Polymarket told CNBC on Tuesday that its annualized revenue had topped $1.8 billion, up from more than $1 billion in June.

Combo contracts, which bundle multiple predictions into a single wager, accounted for $8.6 billion, or 58.2%, of October’s volume. Sports contracts were the next-largest category at $4.57 billion, or 31%.

The platform’s US arm has grown rapidly since the company widened access in May, as states challenge whether federally regulated prediction markets can offer sports contracts without state gambling licenses. Polymarket began admitting US traders to the separate exchange in late 2025, three years after a settlement with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) led it to block US trading on its international platform.

Polymarket US trading volume by category in October 2026. Source: TickerTracker

The growth also follows a surge in sports-related trading during the FIFA World Cup, which ran from June 11 to July 19. Soccer contracts generated $1.81 billion in trading volume in June, up from $85.4 million in May, according to TickerTracker.

Political markets also saw increased activity surrounding the US midterm elections. Election-related contracts generated $108.2 million in trading volume on Polymarket’s US exchange during the first 10 days of November, compared with $16.6 million throughout September. Despite the increase, political markets accounted for just 2.2% of the platform’s November trading volume.

Meanwhile, Polymarket is pursuing a $1 billion funding round at a reported $21 billion post-money valuation. Investment firm 1789 Capital, where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner, is reportedly leading the round with an expected contribution of about $300 million.

Related: Binance, Polymarket seek Polygon hard fork to recover $6.8M in stolen crypto

Despite the figures, Polymarket continues to face regulatory scrutiny on several fronts. The CFTC was reportedly investigating Polymarket earlier this year, while US Senators John Curtis and Adam Schiff separately called on the regulator in June to examine allegations that the company paid social media influencers to promote fabricated trades.

Responding to the allegations, the company told Cointelegraph that it was “conducting a comprehensive audit of active promotional content to ensure it complies with our standards, as well as applicable regulatory and legal disclosure requirements.”

Polymarket is also among several prediction market operators facing legal challenges from US states. New York Attorney General Letitia James sued the company in September, alleging that its sports-related event contracts violated state gambling laws. The lawsuit is part of a broader wave of state actions against prediction market platforms, including Kalshi, over whether their contracts fall under federal commodities regulation or state gambling laws.

The CFTC has defended its authority to regulate prediction markets, pursuing legal action involving 10 states over efforts to enforce state gambling laws against the platforms.

The jurisdictional dispute could ultimately reach the US Supreme Court. In September, New Jersey officials petitioned the court to hear their case against Kalshi, seeking a ruling that could clarify which authorities have jurisdiction over sports-related prediction markets.

#5140. Coinbase Joins Circle, Ripple With Final OCC Approval for Federal Trust Bank Charter

Coinbase Joins Circle, Ripple With Final OCC Approval for Federal Trust Bank Charter

Coinbase has received final approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to charter Coinbase National Trust Company, the crypto exchange said on Monday.

The OCC approved the application last Friday, according to Coinbase. The firm said the charter will let it expand its custody business, which holds digital assets on behalf of institutional clients, under a federal regulatory framework.

"Custody is foundational to our business," the company said, describing itself as the leading crypto custodian globally. The charter will "bring clear and consistent federal uniformity" to its custody operations, it added.

"Trusted custody is essential for bringing more of the financial system onchain," Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong tweeted on Monday, calling the trust company "another step for building that foundation."

Trusted custody is essential for bringing more of the financial system onchain.

Coinbase National Trust Company is another step for building that foundation. https://t.co/35K2yC3xpj

— Brian Armstrong (@brian_armstrong) November 9, 2026

Coinbase has offered regulated custody since 2018, when its Coinbase Custody Trust Company won a limited purpose trust charter from the New York Department of Financial Services. The new national trust company builds on that foundation while bringing its trust activities into a consistent federal framework, Coinbase said.

The approval comes seven months after the OCC gave Coinbase conditional approval in April, when the company said it was not becoming a commercial bank and would not take retail deposits or engage in fractional reserve banking. Coinbase first applied for the charter last year.

Coinbase joins a growing list of crypto firms with national trust charters. Circle won final approval in July for a trust bank to manage the reserves behind its USDC stablecoin, and Ripple received final approval last month for a trust bank behind its RLUSD stablecoin.

Others are still awaiting final approval. Jack Dorsey's Block has applied for a charter to custody Bitcoin in September, Kraken parent Payward filed its own application in May, and a trust company linked to Trump family-backed World Liberty Financial won conditional approval in August for a charter tied to its USD1 stablecoin, Reuters reported.

The approvals have drawn opposition. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) has argued that the OCC's crypto charter approvals, including Coinbase's, are illegal, and the Independent Community Bankers of America has sued the OCC in an effort to stop crypto firms from entering banking through what it describes as a side door.

#5138. Microsoft-Backed Space and Time Launches Platform to Let AI Agents Verify Private Data

Microsoft-Backed Space and Time Launches Platform to Let AI Agents Verify Private Data

Space and Time, a Microsoft-backed blockchain data project, has launched a platform designed to let businesses use private data in AI tools without handing over the underlying records, the company announced on Monday.

Space and Time Enterprise lets companies prove that calculations made on their private data are correct, so that AI applications, auditors and other stakeholders can check the results without accessing the database itself. Launch partners include onchain asset manager Maple Finance, Indonesian vehicle maker and distributor Indomobil, Oracle software consultancy Trenez and AI data network The Data Foundation.

"Businesses want AI agents to execute workflows using that information, but those agents don't need unrestricted access to the records behind every calculation," Nate Holiday, CEO of MakeInfinite Labs, the original developer of Space and Time, told Decrypt.

The stakes are high, he argued. "The potential cost to a business is the overall value of the business," Holiday said. "Giving AI tools unrestricted access to data creates another avenue of exposure."

Holiday said the company is working with customers in industries including construction, engineering and manufacturing that want to rebuild their systems around AI, so that agents, reporting tools and compliance teams can work from the same business records and check the calculations they rely on.

The platform is built on Proof of SQL, Space and Time's patented technology for proving that database queries were computed correctly. It already works with Google Cloud's BigQuery, and businesses can now run it on their own servers without operating a blockchain, buying specialized hardware or relying on an outside proving service, according to the company.

With GPU acceleration, supported queries over millions of rows can be run and proven in under a second, Holiday said, though actual performance depends on the query, hardware and dataset.

The technology proves that a calculation was carried out correctly on a given set of records, but it cannot tell whether those records were accurate to begin with. "An incorrect entry still needs to be caught through the business's data controls," Holiday said, "but verification gives those controls a much stronger foundation: evidence of which data was used and whether it was processed correctly."

Space and Time raised $20 million in 2022 in a strategic funding round led by M12, Microsoft's venture fund. Last year, Grayscale launched a trust giving investors exposure to SXT, the token that powers Space and Time's blockchain. Earlier this year, the company launched Dreamspace, an AI-powered tool built with Microsoft's Azure AI services that lets users create and deploy onchain apps without writing code.

Space and Time also runs SXT Chain, a decentralized network that supplies verifiable data to DeFi, tokenized assets and stablecoins. Asked whether enterprise customers would create demand for SXT, Holiday said businesses could deploy the product in their own environment, and that the network would come into play as their applications "need to connect to onchain markets," with those workloads paid for through Space and Time.

The company's cryptography is also used elsewhere. Microsoft's Nova project includes Blitzar, Space and Time's cryptographic acceleration library, and the team's work on a commitment scheme called Dory contributed to a16z crypto's Jolt proof system, Holiday said.

Over the same dashboard’s seven-day comparisons, spot decentralized exchange turnover fell 5% to $9.9 billion, and stablecoin market capitalization fell 4.38% to $14.5 billion.
